chapters.title: Organisational Behaviour: Significance and Theories
chapters.scope: What organisational behaviour studies, and how management thought moved from efficiency to people to systems and situations.

blocks.title: What organisational behaviour studies
blocks.html:
A bank branch brings in new software, and staff who were steady on the old system start making mistakes and calling in sick. The software works. What needs explaining is how the people responded to it.

In plain wordsOrganisational behaviour (OB) studies how people think, feel and act at work, so that managers can understand it, predict it and improve it.

Exam definitionOrganisational behaviour is a field of study that investigates the impact that individuals, groups and structure have on behaviour within organisations, for the purpose of applying such knowledge toward improving an organisation's effectiveness (Robbins and Judge).

OB works at three levels. The individual level covers personality, perception, attitudes, values, learning and motivation. The group level covers norms, teams, leadership and conflict. The organisation level covers structure, culture and change. OB borrows from psychology, social psychology, sociology, anthropology and political science.

Back to the bank branch. At the individual level, a clerk near retirement may doubt she can learn the software. At the group level, the counter staff may have agreed among themselves to go slow. At the organisation level, head office may have rolled it out with no training. Each level points to a different fix: coaching one person, talking with the group, or paying for training.

The management thought behind OB moved in three steps: from efficiency, to human behaviour, to systems and situational thinking.

SchoolMain focusKey thinkers and theories
ClassicalEfficiency and structureTaylor, Fayol, Weber
BehaviouralPeople and motivationMayo, Maslow, McGregor
ModernSystems and adapting to the situationSystems theory, contingency theory

Don't confuse OB with human resource management (HRM). HRM is a management function: hiring, training, pay and appraisal. OB is the knowledge about behaviour that HRM, and every other manager, draws on.

Where it breaks. OB findings are tendencies that hold on average, not laws that hold for every person. Much of the research was done in North American and European firms, so a finding needs testing before it is applied in an Indian office.

For exams. Match each school to its thinkers: classical with Taylor, Fayol and Weber; behavioural with Mayo, Maslow and McGregor; modern with systems and contingency theory. Know the three levels of analysis and the three aims: understand, predict, improve.

blocks.title: Classical school of management
blocks.html:
An auto-parts plant in Pune ships late every month. Each machinist sets up his lathe his own way, and three supervisors give him different orders. The classical school was built for problems like this.

In plain wordsThe classical school treats an organisation like a well-designed machine: find the best method, divide the work, and make the lines of authority clear.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the classical approach is the earliest modern management thought. It sought the one best way to manage work through efficiency, specialisation, formal structure and a clear chain of command.

It grew up with the Industrial Revolution, when large factories needed ways to organise many workers. Three approaches make it up.

ApproachThinkerCore idea
Scientific managementF. W. TaylorUse scientific methods to find the most efficient way to do a job.
Administrative managementHenri FayolThe management process and general principles of management.
Bureaucratic managementMax WeberA formal organisation run by rules: clear hierarchy, detailed rules and regulations, clear division of labour, a formalised system of operation, impersonality and appointment by professional competence.

Taylor's four principles (The Principles of Scientific Management, 1911):

  1. Science, not rule of thumb.
  2. Scientific selection and training of workers.
  3. Cooperation between workers and management.
  4. Division of work and responsibility: managers plan and train, workers perform.

Taylor's pay idea, worked through. His differential piece-rate paid a higher rate to workers who reached the standard output. As an illustration, say the Pune plant sets a standard of 40 pieces a day. It pays ₹50 a piece to those who reach it and ₹40 a piece to those who do not.

  • A machinist who makes 42 pieces earns 42 × ₹50 = ₹2,100.
  • One who makes 38 pieces earns 38 × ₹40 = ₹1,520.
  • Four pieces apart in output, they are ₹580 apart in pay: the gap pulls workers up to the standard.

Fayol (1916) named five functions of management: planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling. His fourteen principles are division of work; authority and responsibility; discipline; unity of command; unity of direction; and subordination of individual interest to the general interest. The rest are remuneration; centralisation; scalar chain; order; equity; stability of tenure; initiative; and esprit de corps. In the Pune plant, unity of command would give each machinist one supervisor.

Weber's aim was efficiency and an end to favouritism. In a bureaucracy, a machinist is promoted because he passes a skills test, not because he is related to the plant head.

Don't confuse Taylor with Fayol. Taylor worked from the shop floor up: the best way to do one task. Fayol worked from the top down: what every manager does. Unity of command is Fayol's principle. Taylor's functional foremanship, which put eight specialist foremen over each worker, breaks it.

Where it breaks. The classical school treated workers as parts of a machine, moved mainly by pay. It ignored feelings, informal groups and the world outside the organisation. In a bureaucracy, rules can become goals in themselves, which is what people mean by red tape.

In practice. Shop-floor procedures, hospital checklists and a public-sector bank's written rules are classical ideas still at work. They suit repeated tasks where errors are costly.

For exams. Expect Taylor's principles and techniques (time study, motion study, functional foremanship, differential piece-rate), Fayol's five functions and fourteen principles, and Weber's features of bureaucracy. Theories of management (Unit 1) treats each thinker in more depth.

Taylor the task, Fayol the manager, Weber the rules.

blocks.title: Behavioural school of management
blocks.html:
A plant manager raises pay and brightens the lighting, but output barely moves. Meanwhile a team whose supervisor listens and praises keeps beating its targets. The behavioural school set out to explain why.

In plain wordsThe behavioural school says people at work are not machine parts: their feelings, needs and relationships drive how hard and how well they work.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the behavioural approach studies human behaviour at work, such as motivation, group relations and leadership. It holds that productivity depends on social and psychological factors as well as on the design of work.

It began as a reaction to the limits of the classical approach. Three bodies of work define it.

1. The Hawthorne studies ran from 1924 to 1932 at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago. Elton Mayo and his Harvard colleagues interpreted them. They ran in four phases.

  • Illumination experiments: output rose in both the test group and the control group, whether the lighting went up or down. Something other than light was at work.
  • Relay assembly test room: a small group of women had their breaks and hours changed. Output rose through most changes, and stayed high when the old conditions returned.
  • Interviewing programme: thousands of employees were interviewed. Being listened to improved morale.
  • Bank wiring observation room: a group of men set their own output norm and pressed anyone who worked too fast or too slow.

The conclusion: social needs, morale and relationships shape behaviour at work, and productivity rose when employees felt valued. The Hawthorne effect is the change in behaviour that comes from attention, including being observed.

2. Maslow's hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation. Managers should understand and address the different needs employees have. Values, learning and motivation (this unit) explains it in full.

3. McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y (The Human Side of Enterprise, 1960): two opposite sets of assumptions a manager may hold about people at work.

AspectTheory XTheory Y
View of workEmployees dislike workEmployees can be motivated
DirectionPeople need coercion and controlPeople can direct themselves and seek responsibility
StyleManagement-centred controlParticipative management
TrustLowTrust and collaboration
CreativityAssumed to be limitedEncouraged

An example. Two managers run branches of the same public-sector bank. The first checks every voucher himself and lets no officer decide anything alone: Theory X. The second agrees targets with her officers and lets them choose how to meet them: Theory Y.

Don't confuse Theory X and Y with two types of worker. They are a manager's assumptions about workers. McGregor's point was that assumptions tend to fulfil themselves: treat people as lazy and they disengage. Theory Z is a separate idea, William Ouchi's 1981 account of Japanese-style management.

Where it breaks. The Hawthorne groups were small and the controls weak, and later re-analyses of the data questioned how much attention alone raised output. A happy worker is not always a productive one. Research gives little support to Maslow's strict order of needs.

For exams. Know the four Hawthorne phases in order, the meaning of the Hawthorne effect, Maslow's five levels, and the Theory X and Theory Y contrast.

The core contrast: control against participation.

blocks.title: Modern school: systems and contingency
blocks.html:
A rule book that suits Indian Railways would smother a two-person chai stall, and the stall's easy habits could not run a railway. The modern school asks what fits each case.

In plain wordsThe modern school sees an organisation as connected parts that trade with their surroundings, and says the right way to manage depends on the situation.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a system is a set of interrelated and interdependent parts arranged to produce a unified whole. The contingency approach holds that organisations differ, face different situations, and so require different ways of managing.

The modern school recognises how complex organisations are, and how much they depend on their environment.

Systems theory sees the organisation as an open system. Inputs (labour, materials, capital) pass through a transformation process (activities and operations) to become outputs (products and services). Feedback returns to the start, all within an external environment. The parts are interrelated and work toward a common goal. The key ideas are interdependence, interaction, environment and feedback.

An example. A district milk cooperative takes in milk, labour and capital, then chills, tests and packs the milk for shops. Shops report that one pack size goes unsold, and the cooperative changes its packing. A weak monsoon or a new rival brand, both in the environment, can upset every part at once.

Contingency theory holds that there is no single best way to manage: practice must be tailored to the situation. Effectiveness depends on the external environment, technology, organisational structure and the characteristics of the workforce. Research found, for example, that tight, rule-bound (mechanistic) structures suit stable markets, while flexible (organic) structures suit fast-changing ones.

The manager works in four steps:

  1. Analyse the situation.
  2. Identify the variables that matter.
  3. Adapt the practice to fit them.
  4. Act, and watch the results.

Don't confuse systems theory with contingency theory. Systems theory describes how the parts of an organisation connect with each other and the environment. Contingency theory tells a manager how to choose a practice: by reading the situation. A closed system, by contrast, ignores its environment, as the classical school largely did.

Where it breaks. "It depends" helps only when the manager knows what it depends on. Systems theory can describe almost anything and prescribe very little. And contingency does not mean "anything goes": some choices fit a situation and others do not.

For exams. Know input, transformation, output and feedback; open against closed systems; and contingency as "no one best way". Expect Ludwig von Bertalanffy with general systems theory, and Burns and Stalker, Joan Woodward, and Lawrence and Lorsch with contingency research.

Go deeper for practitioners

Open-system terms. Ludwig von Bertalanffy developed general systems theory in biology. Daniel Katz and Robert Kahn applied open-system thinking to organisations in the 1960s. Three terms recur: synergy, the whole achieving more than its parts alone; entropy, the tendency of a closed system to run down; and equifinality, reaching the same end by different paths.

Three contingency studies. Tom Burns and G. M. Stalker (1961) found mechanistic structures suited stable markets and organic structures suited changing ones. Joan Woodward linked the best structure to a firm's production technology: unit, mass or process production. Paul Lawrence and Jay Lorsch (1967) showed that firms in uncertain environments need more difference between departments, and stronger ways to integrate them.

A decision. A family-run kirana business grows from one store to twenty across two cities. The founder still approves every purchase himself. Contingency thinking asks what changed: size, distance and the number of suppliers. Which decisions should move to store managers, and which rules must stay the same in every store?

Links. Organisation structure (Unit 1) covers mechanistic and organic designs; Group behaviour, teams and leadership (this unit) covers Fiedler's contingency model of leadership.

It depends on the situation.

text: Kauṭilya's accounts office (akṣapaṭala) keeps registers for every department, fixes when and how accounts are to be presented, and sets penalties for officials who fail to present them. Written records, set procedures and regular checks are what Weber later described as bureaucracy.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.7

text: Theory Y assumes that people can direct themselves and will seek responsibility. The Gītā asks each person to raise themselves by their own effort and not let themselves sink, which treats self-direction as a human capacity. The verse is about inner discipline, not about a manager's assumptions.
pairings.quote: “Lift yourself by yourself; do not let yourself sink.” उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । uddhared ātmanātmānaṃ nātmānam avasādayet. Bhagavad Gītā 6.5

chapters.title: Personality, Perception and Attitude
chapters.scope: Who a person is, how they read the world, and the stance they take toward it: three building blocks of individual behaviour at work.

blocks.title: Personality
blocks.html:
Two equally qualified officers join a bank branch. One takes every customer complaint in her stride; the other loses sleep over each one. Their skills are the same; their personalities differ.

In plain wordsPersonality is a person's typical way of thinking, feeling and acting, which stays fairly steady across situations and over time.

Exam definitionPersonality is the sum total of ways in which an individual reacts to and interacts with others (Robbins and Judge).

Personality is unique to each person and relatively consistent. It is shaped by genetics, environment, experience and learning. At work it matters for recruitment, communication, team dynamics, leadership, motivation, job satisfaction and performance.

The Big Five (OCEAN) is the trait model with the strongest research support. Each trait is a scale, and every person sits somewhere along it.

TraitHigh scorers tend to beAt work
OpennessCurious, imaginative, open to new ideasAdapt well to change and creative work
ConscientiousnessOrganised, dependable, persistentThe most consistent link with job performance across many jobs
ExtraversionSociable, assertive, talkativeSuit roles with much contact; often emerge as leaders
AgreeablenessCooperative, warm, trustingGood team members; may avoid needed conflict
NeuroticismAnxious, insecure, moodyLow scorers, who are emotionally stable, cope better with stress

An example. On a college fest committee, the highly conscientious member keeps the budget, and the extravert handles sponsors. The member high on openness designs the new event.

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), developed by Katharine Briggs and Isabel Myers from Carl Jung's psychological types, sorts people into types along four dimensions. Each dimension is a two-way choice, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 types. ESTJ, for example, is extraversion, sensing, thinking and judging. It is used to understand team compatibility, leadership styles and communication preferences.

DimensionOne preferenceThe other
E – IExtraversion: interaction, outward energyIntroversion: reflection, solitude
S – NSensing: facts and present realitiesIntuition: patterns and possibilities
T – FThinking: logic and objectivityFeeling: empathy and human impact
J – PJudging: structure and decisivenessPerceiving: flexibility and spontaneity
TheoryProponentsCore idea
PsychoanalyticSigmund FreudUnconscious conflicts among id, ego and superego; early childhood shapes personality.
BehaviouristB. F. Skinner, J. B. WatsonPersonality develops through learning, conditioning and reinforcement.
HumanisticCarl Rogers, Abraham MaslowPeople strive for self-growth and to fulfil their potential.
TraitGordon Allport; the Big FivePersonality is a set of relatively stable traits.
CognitiveAlbert BanduraMental processes, observation, imitation and self-efficacy shape personality.
BiologicalHans Eysenck; Darwinian viewPersonality is linked to genetics, brain chemistry and evolution.

Don't confuse the MBTI with the Big Five. The MBTI sorts people into types: you are E or I. The Big Five scores each trait on a scale: you are more or less extraverted. Neuroticism is not an illness; it is the low end of emotional stability.

Where it breaks. The MBTI is popular in training, but its types predict job performance poorly, and people often get a different type when retested. Traits predict behaviour on average, not in every situation. Strong situations, such as strict rules or an emergency, override personality.

In practice. Use personality to place and develop people, not to label them. In hiring, a validated measure of conscientiousness tells you more than an MBTI type.

Go deeper for practitioners

Other traits exams ask about.

  • Locus of control (Julian Rotter): internals believe they control what happens to them; externals credit luck or other people.
  • Type A and Type B (Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman): Type A people are impatient, competitive and hurried; Type B people are relaxed.
  • Self-monitoring (Mark Snyder): high self-monitors adjust their behaviour to the situation; low self-monitors act the same everywhere.
  • Machiavellianism: pragmatic, emotionally distant, and willing to believe that ends justify means.
  • Self-esteem: how far people like or dislike themselves.

A decision. You are hiring ten officers for a new branch. A vendor offers an MBTI workshop to "find the right types". Evidence favours structured interviews and a validated conscientiousness measure for selection. The MBTI may still help a team talk about how its members prefer to work.

Personality is who you are, fairly steadily, from one situation to the next.

blocks.title: Perception
blocks.html:
In an appraisal meeting, one manager sees a confident young officer who speaks well. Another sees someone who talks more than he delivers. Same person, same year's work, two readings.

In plain wordsPerception is how we make sense of what we see and hear: we pick out some of it, sort it, and give it meaning.

Exam definitionPerception is a process by which individuals organise and interpret their sensory impressions in order to give meaning to their environment (Robbins and Judge).

Perception is subjective: the same situation can draw different responses because people's experiences and expectations differ. People act on what they perceive, not on what is objectively there.

StageWhat happens
1 SelectionWe notice only some of the many stimuli, influenced by intensity, relevance, novelty, interests and expectations.
2 OrganisationWe arrange what we noticed into patterns, by similarity, proximity and closure.
3 InterpretationWe give it meaning using experience, beliefs and motives. Assumptions and stereotypes creep in here.

Three sets of factors shape perception: the perceiver (motives, experiences, attitudes, expectations), the target (appearance, behaviour, communication style) and the situation (context, time, work setting).

Attribution theory (Harold Kelley) explains how we judge the cause of someone's behaviour. Was it internal, coming from the person, or external, coming from the situation? We use three cues.

CueThe questionIf high, we lean toward
DistinctivenessDoes the person act differently in different situations?External cause
ConsensusDo others act the same way in the same situation?External cause
ConsistencyDoes the person act the same way over time?Internal cause

An example. An officer reaches the branch an hour late. If most of the staff were late that morning, consensus is high, and the manager blames the traffic. If she is often late, and late for meetings too, consistency is high and distinctiveness low. Then the manager blames her.

Perceptual errorWhat happens
StereotypingJudging a person by the group they belong to.
Halo effectOne favourable trait shapes the whole judgement.
Horn effectOne unfavourable trait shapes the whole judgement.
Selective perceptionNoticing only what supports opinions already held.
ProjectionAttributing one's own thoughts, feelings or motives to others.
Contrast effectJudging a person against others rather than against an objective standard.
Fundamental attribution errorBlaming others' behaviour on their character and underrating the situation.
Self-serving biasCrediting our own successes to ourselves and blaming our failures on circumstances.

In the appraisal meeting, the first manager may show a halo effect: good speaking colours the whole rating. A related error is judging an idea by who said it, rather than by its merits.

Don't confuse the halo effect with stereotyping. The halo effect spreads one trait of a person across the whole judgement of that person. Stereotyping judges a person by the group they belong to. Likewise, the fundamental attribution error is about how we judge others; the self-serving bias is about how we judge ourselves.

Where it breaks. Good intentions do not remove these errors, because they work below awareness. Process does more: structured interviews with the same questions for everyone, written criteria, and more than one rater.

In practice. Perception decides hiring, appraisals and promotions. Before rating someone, ask which cue you used and what evidence you have from the whole period.

Go deeper for practitioners

The self-fulfilling prophecy. What we expect of people can shape what they do. In Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson's classroom study, published in 1968, teachers were told that some pupils, in fact chosen at random, would bloom. Those pupils gained more on a later test. This is called the Pygmalion effect. Later studies found the effect real but usually smaller. A manager who expects little from a new officer may give her less attention and fewer chances, and so get less.

A decision. Your best salesperson misses target for one quarter. Everyone else in the region also fell short, after a competitor cut prices. Consensus is high, so the situation is the likelier cause. Blaming her effort would be the fundamental attribution error, and could cost you a strong performer.

Select, organise, interpret.

blocks.title: Attitude
blocks.html:
A kirana store's new assistant believes customers should be served well, yet he feels irritated by them and avoids the counter. What he thinks, what he feels and what he does do not line up. Attitude theory explains how they fit together.

In plain wordsAn attitude is a settled liking or disliking for something, such as a job, a boss or a policy. It is made of what you think, what you feel and what you are ready to do.

Exam definitionAttitudes are evaluative statements, either favourable or unfavourable, about objects, people or events (Robbins and Judge).

An attitude is a learned tendency to respond consistently, in a favourable or unfavourable way. It combines beliefs, feelings and an intention to behave. It influences job satisfaction, motivation and organisational commitment.

ComponentWhat it isExample
AffectiveFeelings and emotions: liking, disliking, indifference“I enjoy this project.”
BehaviouralAn intention or readiness to actWorking overtime to reach a goal
CognitiveBeliefs and ideas“Hard work leads to success.”

Cognitive is what you think, affective what you feel, behavioural what you are ready to do.

Cognitive dissonance. Leon Festinger (1957) showed that people feel uncomfortable when their attitudes clash with each other or with their behaviour. They reduce the discomfort by changing the attitude, changing the behaviour, or explaining the clash away. The kirana assistant might decide that "difficult customers are not worth serving well", which changes the belief to fit the behaviour.

Three attitudes matter most at work.

  • Job satisfaction is the positive or negative feeling toward one's job, role and work environment. High satisfaction supports commitment and performance.
  • Organisational commitment is emotional attachment and loyalty to the organisation. Strong commitment can reduce turnover and absenteeism. John Meyer and Natalie Allen describe three forms: affective (I want to stay), continuance (I need to stay) and normative (I ought to stay).
  • Job involvement is how far a person identifies with their job and treats it as important to their self-worth.

Why it costs money. As an illustration, suppose a branch of 20 staff loses 5 people a year. If replacing each costs about ₹2 lakh in hiring and training, turnover costs 5 × ₹2 lakh = ₹10 lakh a year. Raising commitment so that only 2 leave would save 3 × ₹2 lakh = ₹6 lakh.

Attitudes are formed by family and early experience, by peer groups and society, by the organisational environment (leadership, rewards, recognition, communication) and by personal experience of success and failure.

Don't confuse job involvement with organisational commitment. Involvement is attachment to the job itself; commitment is attachment to the employer. A doctor can be deeply involved in medicine and still feel no loyalty to the hospital that employs her.

Where it breaks. Attitudes predict behaviour only loosely. The link is stronger when the attitude is strong, specific to the behaviour and based on direct experience. It is weaker when social pressure pushes the other way. Across many studies, satisfaction and performance are only moderately related, and a satisfied employee may still leave for better pay.

In practice. Attitude surveys show where trouble is building before people leave. Robbins and Judge sort responses to dissatisfaction into four kinds: exit (leaving), voice (speaking up), loyalty (waiting for things to improve) and neglect (letting work slide).

For exams. Know the three components and match examples to them, the three work attitudes, Festinger's cognitive dissonance, and Meyer and Allen's three forms of commitment.

text: The Gītā describes three qualities born of nature (sattva, rajas and tamas) that bind every person and mix in different proportions, and later sorts food, work and faith by them. A modern reader may see a trait theory: stable dispositions that shape behaviour. The guṇas are a metaphysical account, not a measured personality test.
pairings.quote: “Sattva, rajas and tamas, the qualities born of nature, bind the embodied self.” सत्त्वं रजस्तम इति गुणाः प्रकृतिसम्भवाः । sattvaṃ rajas tama iti guṇāḥ prakṛti-sambhavāḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 14.5

text: Personality is defined as a relatively consistent pattern. The Gītā observes that even a wise person acts in keeping with their own nature, and that all beings follow theirs: a person's disposition persists from one situation to the next.
pairings.quote: “Even the wise act in keeping with their own nature; beings follow their nature.” सदृशं चेष्टते स्वस्याः प्रकृतेर्ज्ञानवानपि । प्रकृतिं यान्ति भूतानि । sadṛśaṃ ceṣṭate svasyāḥ prakṛter jñānavān api, prakṛtiṃ yānti bhūtāni. Bhagavad Gītā 3.33

text: Tiruvaḷḷuvar's advice for judging people is to look for their merits, then for their faults, and to judge by whichever outweighs the other. It is a direct guard against the halo and horn effects, where one trait decides the whole judgement.
pairings.quote: “Examine a person's merits, examine their faults too, and judge by whichever is greater.” குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி அவற்றுள் மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 504

pairings.modern: Judging the message by the speaker
text: The Kuṟaḷ defines wisdom as finding the truth of what is said, whoever says it. Judging a message by its source (a respected senior, an unpopular colleague) is a common perceptual error at work.
pairings.quote: “Whatever is heard, from whomever, wisdom is to discern the truth in it.” எப்பொருள் யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 423

pairings.classic: a person is made of their faith
text: The Gītā says each person's faith takes the shape of their nature, and that a person is made of their faith. Attitude theory makes a narrower claim, a learned tendency to respond in a consistent way, but both see a settled inner stance shaping action.
pairings.quote: “A person is made of their faith: as their faith is, so are they.” श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः । śraddhāmayo ’yaṃ puruṣo yo yac-chraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 17.3

text: The Dhammapada observes that people see others' faults easily and their own with difficulty, sifting the first like chaff and hiding the second like a gambler hiding a losing throw. That is the asymmetry attribution research later measured: we explain others' failures by their character and our own by circumstance.
pairings.quote: “The faults of others are easy to see, one's own hard to see. One winnows others' faults like chaff, but hides one's own, as a cheat hides a losing throw.” सुदस्सं वज्जमञ्ञेसं । अत्तनो पन दुद्दसं । परेसं हि सो वज्जानि ओपुनाति यथा भुसं । अत्तनो पन छादेति कलिं व कितवा सठो । sudassaṃ vajjam aññesaṃ, attano pana duddasaṃ; paresaṃ hi so vajjāni opunāti yathā bhusaṃ; attano pana chādeti kaliṃ va kitavā saṭho. Dhammapada 252 (Pali)

chapters.title: Values, Learning and Motivation
chapters.scope: What shapes individual behaviour, the values people steer by, how they learn, and what moves them to act.

blocks.title: What shapes individual behaviour
blocks.html:
Two probationary officers join the same public-sector bank branch on the same day, after the same training. At the first quarter-end, one treats the deposit target as a game to win; the other is anxious for weeks. Same job, same rules, different behaviour.

In plain wordsIndividual behaviour is what a person does, says and feels at work, and the reasons behind it.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: individual behaviour is the way a person acts, thinks and responds, shaped by internal traits, learned experience and the surroundings.

Understanding it helps a manager explain people's reactions, and improve how the organisation works. Kurt Lewin put the idea as a formula in 1936:

B = f(P, E): behaviour is a function of the person and the environment

Neither part works alone. The same person behaves differently in a different setting, and the same setting draws different behaviour from different people. The factors fall into three groups.

FactorWhat it includesAt work
BiologicalAge, gender, health, heredityPhysical and emotional abilities; adaptability and handling of stress may vary.
PsychologicalPersonality, perception, attitude, beliefsAn optimistic employee may see a deadline as a challenge rather than a threat.
EnvironmentalCulture, family, peers, workplaceCollectivist cultures stress teamwork; individualist cultures stress personal success.

Back to the bank branch. The two officers are of the same age and in good health, so biology explains little here. Psychology explains more: the first officer is optimistic and sees the target as a challenge. The environment adds the rest: perhaps she grew up in a family business where targets were dinner-table talk. Both work under the same branch manager, whose style also shapes them.

Don't confuse behaviour with personality. Personality is the stable pattern of traits a person carries; it is one psychological factor. Behaviour is what the person actually does in a given situation, and it depends on the setting too.

Where it breaks. The three groups act together, so their effects can rarely be separated. Factors that are easy to see, such as age and gender, tempt managers to stereotype; reviews of the research find few consistent differences between men and women in job performance. Culture labels such as "collectivist" describe averages across a country, not any one person.

In practice. A manager cannot change a person's heredity or upbringing, but can change the environment: the job, the team, the targets and the rewards. So the useful question is which part of the situation to change.

For exams. Know the three groups of factors with their examples, and Lewin's B = f(P, E). Individualism and collectivism come from Hofstede's work, covered in Workforce Diversity and Cross-Cultural Behaviour.

blocks.title: Values
blocks.html:
A borrower whose loan file is pending brings the branch's loan officer an expensive Diwali gift. Politeness says accept it; honesty says refuse it. Which way she goes depends on her values.

In plain wordsValues are a person's settled beliefs about what matters and what is right.

Exam definitionA value is an enduring belief that a specific mode of conduct or end-state of existence is personally or socially preferable to an opposite or converse mode of conduct or end-state of existence (Milton Rokeach).

Values guide actions and decisions: what a person considers right, desirable or important. They:

  • are stable and enduring, often formed early through family and culture;
  • act as standards for judging actions and people;
  • influence ethical behaviour and responsibility;
  • shape priorities in life and work.

Rokeach's definition has two halves, and they give his two types of value. An end-state of existence is a terminal value; a mode of conduct is an instrumental value. His Rokeach Value Survey lists 18 of each and asks people to rank them.

Rokeach's value typesMeaningExamples
Terminal valuesEnd goals a person strives forFreedom, inner harmony, wisdom
Instrumental valuesThe means, or principles, used to reach themHonesty, responsibility, politeness

Back to the loan officer. Two of her instrumental values, honesty and politeness, pull in opposite directions. The ranking settles it. If honesty ranks above politeness, she refuses the gift, politely.

Don't confuse values with attitudes. A value is broad and stable: "honesty matters". An attitude is an evaluation of one particular thing: "I dislike the new gift policy". Attitudes change more easily. Nor terminal with instrumental: ask whether it is a state you want to reach (terminal) or a way you behave (instrumental).

Where it breaks. Stated values do not always predict behaviour. Pressure, incentives and the situation act too, so a person who ranks honesty first on a survey may still bend under a tough target. Values are stable, not fixed: they shift slowly across a life, and rankings differ between cultures and generations.

In practice. Organisations turn instrumental values into rules, such as a gift policy with a clear limit, so that no one has to weigh honesty against politeness at the counter. Values printed on a wall poster change little unless people are rewarded for living them.

For exams. Terminal values are ends, instrumental values are means, and the Rokeach Value Survey has 18 of each. Another classic scheme, by Allport, Vernon and Lindzey, sorts values into six types: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political and religious.

Terminal values are ends; instrumental values are means.

blocks.title: Learning
blocks.html:
A new machine operator at a Pune auto-parts plant is safe and fast within three months. Part of that came from training, part from watching the senior on the next machine, and part from the supervisor's praise. Learning theories separate these routes.

In plain wordsLearning is a lasting change in what a person does or knows, caused by experience.

Exam definitionLearning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour that occurs as a result of experience (Robbins and Judge).

"Relatively permanent" rules out changes that pass, such as tiredness or illness. Learning comes from experience, observation or practice, and it builds adaptability and competence. It can be active or passive, intentional or unintentional; it is lifelong; and it changes thoughts, attitudes and skills. Four theories explain how it happens.

TheoryKey ideaExampleAt work
Classical conditioning (Pavlov)Learning by association between a neutral stimulus and a natural responseA school bell comes to signal lunch, and hungerAdvertising links emotions with products
Operant conditioning (Skinner)Behaviour shaped by rewards and punishmentsPraise for an early submission makes it more likely againBonuses encourage performance
Cognitive learning (Tolman, Piaget)Learning through reasoning, thinking and problem-solvingMind maps to understand a topicCase analysis in corporate training
Social learning (Bandura)Learning by observing and imitating othersA new employee copies a punctual seniorRole models shape habits

Classical conditioning. Food makes a dog salivate without any learning. Ivan Pavlov sounded a bell just before feeding, many times. In the end the bell alone made the dogs salivate. The response is involuntary: the person, or the dog, does not choose it.

Operant conditioning. B. F. Skinner showed that behaviour followed by a pleasant result tends to be repeated, and behaviour followed by nothing, or by an unpleasant result, tends to fade. A manager has four ways to use this.

MethodWhat the manager doesEffect on the behaviourAt the Pune plant
Positive reinforcementAdds something pleasantMore likelyPraise for a shift with no safety lapse
Negative reinforcementRemoves something unpleasantMore likelyDaily checks on an operator stop once his scrap rate falls
PunishmentAdds something unpleasantLess likelyA written warning for skipping safety gloves
ExtinctionWithholds the usual rewardFadesThe supervisor stops laughing at jokes that derail meetings

Social learning. Albert Bandura showed that people also learn by watching others and seeing what happens to them. It works through four processes: attention to the model, retention of what was seen, reproduction of the behaviour, and reinforcement that makes it worth repeating.

Don't confuse negative reinforcement with punishment. Both involve something unpleasant. Negative reinforcement removes it, to make a behaviour more likely. Punishment adds it, to make a behaviour less likely. Nor classical with operant conditioning: classical works on involuntary reactions to what comes before; operant works on chosen behaviour, through what comes after.

Where it breaks. Conditioning theories grew from animal experiments and say little about thinking; cognitive and social learning fill that gap. Punishment tells people what not to do, but not what to do, and it can breed fear and resentment.

In practice. Reward the behaviour you want soon after it happens. Give each new joiner a good model to watch, such as a buddy. Build practice and feedback into training, not only lectures.

Go deeper for practitioners

Schedules of reinforcement. Rewarding every correct act (continuous reinforcement) teaches fast, but the behaviour fades quickly once rewards stop. Rewarding only some acts (intermittent reinforcement) comes in four schedules.

ScheduleThe reward comes…Example
Fixed-intervalafter a set timeA monthly salary
Variable-intervalafter varying, unpredictable timesPraise during surprise quality audits
Fixed-ratioafter a set number of responsesPiece-rate pay: a fixed sum per 100 parts
Variable-ratioafter a varying number of responsesSales commission: some calls end in a sale, most do not

Variable schedules tend to produce steadier effort, and behaviour that lasts longer once rewards stop. A fixed salary rewards turning up, not any particular piece of work.

A decision. Operators skip safety gloves on hot days. A fine is punishment: it may stop the behaviour while the supervisor is watching. Praising a crew for each glove-compliant week is positive reinforcement, and a respected senior who always wears them is a model to copy. Which do you try first?

Links. Personality, Perception and Attitude (this unit) uses Skinner's and Bandura's ideas to explain how personality forms. Consumer and Industrial Buying Behaviour (Unit 7) includes a Pavlovian learning model of the buyer.

Pavlov associates, Skinner reinforces, Piaget thinks, Bandura watches.

blocks.title: Motivation
blocks.html:
A two-wheeler showroom pays all its sales executives under the same bonus scheme. Three months later, one sells twice as many bikes as the others. Same scheme, different effort: motivation theory asks what moves people, and how.

In plain wordsMotivation is what makes a person start working towards a goal, aim the effort, and keep it up.

Exam definitionMotivation is the processes that account for an individual's intensity, direction and persistence of effort toward attaining a goal (Robbins and Judge).

It is an internal or external push. It energises behaviour (intensity), guides it (direction) and sustains it (persistence). The theories fall into two families. Content theories ask what motivates: Maslow, Herzberg and McClelland. Process theories ask how motivation works: Vroom.

TheoryCore ideaAt work
Maslow's hierarchy of needsNeeds rise from physiological, to safety, to social, to esteem, to self-actualisationMatch benefits and incentives to the needs employees have now
Herzberg's two-factor theoryMotivators create satisfaction; hygiene factors only prevent dissatisfactionPay is a hygiene factor; recognition is a motivator
McClelland's needs theoryBehaviour is driven by the needs for achievement, affiliation and powerAssign work to suit the dominant need
Vroom's expectancy theoryEffort leads to performance, and performance to rewardClear goals and valued rewards strengthen motivation

Maslow (1943). Physiological and safety needs are lower-order needs; social, esteem and self-actualisation needs are higher-order. A new executive worried about rent responds to a steady salary; one secure in her job responds more to recognition and growth.

Herzberg. Satisfaction and dissatisfaction are not two ends of one scale. The opposite of satisfaction is no satisfaction; the opposite of dissatisfaction is no dissatisfaction.

Hygiene factorsMotivators
Company policy, supervision, pay, relations with colleagues, working conditionsAchievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth
Poor ones cause dissatisfaction; good ones only remove itPresent ones create satisfaction and effort

McClelland. The three needs are learned, and one usually dominates. A person high in the need for achievement likes moderate risks, personal responsibility and quick feedback, so give that person a target and a scoreboard.

Vroom (1964). A person weighs three links before putting in effort.

Motivation = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence

Worked example. The showroom offers ₹20,000 to anyone who sells 30 bikes in a month. One executive judges her chance of reaching 30 with extra effort at 0.8 (E). The showroom has paid such bonuses reliably, so she puts I at 0.9. She would rather have time off than money, so V = 0.5. Each is scored from 0 to 1, as an illustration.

  • Motivation = 0.8 × 0.9 × 0.5 = 0.72 × 0.5 = 0.36.
  • If the showroom had never paid a promised bonus, she would put I at 0. Then motivation = 0.8 × 0 × 0.5 = 0, however reachable the target.

Because the links multiply, one weak link pulls the whole result down.

Don't confuse content theories with process theories. Content theories list what motivates; process theories explain how the decision to make an effort is made. Nor hygiene factors with unimportant ones: they do not motivate, but get them wrong and people become dissatisfied.

Where it breaks. Research gives little support to Maslow's strict order; people pursue several needs at once. Herzberg drew his factors from interviews about good and bad times at work. People tend to credit themselves for good times and blame their surroundings for bad ones, which may have produced the split. McClelland's needs are measured with projective tests such as the Thematic Apperception Test, which are hard to score consistently. Vroom assumes people calculate; real choices are rougher.

In practice. Diagnose before acting. Is the problem dissatisfaction, which better hygiene factors would remove, or missing motivators? Under Vroom, which link is weak: E, I or V?

For exams. Know Maslow's five levels in order, Herzberg's two lists, McClelland's three needs and Vroom's formula, and which theories are content and which process.

Go deeper for practitioners

Alderfer's ERG theory regroups Maslow's needs into three: existence, relatedness and growth. Several needs can act at once. When a higher need is frustrated, a person may fall back on a lower one: an executive who sees no path to promotion may push harder for pay.

Herzberg's study (1959) asked about 200 engineers and accountants to describe times they felt especially good or bad about their jobs. Good times were mostly about the work itself; bad times mostly about the surroundings.

A decision. Two showroom executives are both underperforming. One says the target cannot be reached: expectancy is low, so give training or a nearer target. The other says bonuses are always paid late: instrumentality is low, so fix the payment. The same bonus scheme fails for two different reasons.

Links. House's path–goal theory of leadership, in Group Behaviour, Teams and Leadership, builds on expectancy theory. Job enrichment, in Job Analysis, Evaluation and Design, builds on Herzberg's motivators.

text: Manu lists ten marks of dharma: steadiness, forgiveness, self-control, not stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness and freedom from anger. Most are ways of acting rather than end goals, close to Rokeach's instrumental values such as honesty and responsibility. Manu does not divide ends from means this way, so the comparison is a reading.

text: Patañjali says practice becomes firmly grounded when it is kept up for a long time, without interruption and with care. Learning theory describes the same result, a lasting change through practice, and adds that rewards and observation also shape it.
pairings.quote: “Practice becomes firmly grounded when it is pursued for a long time, without a break, and with devotion.” स तु दीर्घकालनैरन्तर्यसत्कारासेवितो दृढभूमिः । sa tu dīrgha-kāla-nairantarya-satkārāsevito dṛḍha-bhūmiḥ. Yoga Sūtra 1.14

text: Bandura's social learning theory holds that people learn by watching and imitating others. The Gītā observes that people do what the best among them do, and follow the standard those people set.
pairings.quote: “Whatever the best person does, others do too; the world follows the standard they set.” यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः । स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते । yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas tat tad evetaro janaḥ, sa yat pramāṇaṃ kurute lokas tad anuvartate. Bhagavad Gītā 3.21

text: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad describes the person as five layers, each within the last: food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss. A modern reader may see Maslow's climb from physiological needs to self-actualisation. The Upaniṣad describes the self, not a sequence of needs at work, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Within it is another self.” अन्योऽन्तर आत्मा । anyo ’ntara ātmā. Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1–2.5

text: The Kuṟaḷ says that effort creates prosperity and the lack of it brings poverty. Vroom's expectancy theory asks whether people believe effort will lead to performance and performance to reward. The couplet states the first link with confidence; the theory treats it as a belief that may be weak.
pairings.quote: “Effort brings prosperity; the absence of effort brings poverty.” முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 616

chapters.title: Group Behaviour, Teams and Leadership
chapters.scope: How people act together: kinds of groups and their norms, how teams develop, how leaders lead, and the forces at work inside a group.

blocks.title: Groups and group norms
blocks.html:
Put five capable people in a room and they behave differently than they would alone: some go quiet, some go along, some ease off. Group behaviour is the study of why.

In plain wordsA group is a few people who deal with each other and need each other to get something done.

Exam definitionA group is two or more individuals, interacting and interdependent, who have come together to achieve particular objectives (Robbins and Judge).

Group behaviour is how individuals act, interact and influence one another within a group, through shared goals, roles, communication and social influence. Belonging to a group can change a person's behaviour, attitudes and decisions.

Formal or informalFormal groupsInformal groups
How they formDeliberately created by the organisationNaturally and spontaneously
BasisStructured roles and assigned tasksShared interests and social relationships
AimSpecific organisational objectivesNot bound by the official structure
ExampleThe finance departmentColleagues who share a lunch table or a cricket team

Group norms are the unwritten rules that guide behaviour and set shared expectations. Positive norms bring harmony and productivity; negative norms bring excessive pressure and lower performance. Example: members mute their phones in meetings without being asked.

Social loafing is putting in less effort in a group than when working alone, on the assumption that others will make up for it. Group performance falls, and so does the motivation of the committed members. Example: two students doing most of a group case study. Maximilien Ringelmann's rope-pulling experiments in the late 1800s first showed it: the more people pulled, the less each pulled. It shrinks when each person's contribution is visible, teams are small, and the task matters to them.

Don't confuse a group with a team. Every team is a group, but not every group is a team. In a team, members share responsibility for one result; in a work group, each answers for their own part.

blocks.title: Team building and Tuckman's stages
blocks.html:
New teams almost always hit a rough patch a few weeks in. Tuckman's stages say that is normal, and show what helps at each point.

Team building is a deliberate process of building trust, collaboration and agreement on goals. It runs from trust, to communication, to resolving conflict, to collaboration, to shared goals. It brings trust and empathy, creativity, better communication and better problem-solving.

Bruce Tuckman described four stages in 1965; with Mary Ann Jensen he added a fifth, adjourning, in 1977. Think of a college fest committee: excited first meetings, a row over the budget, agreed ground rules, a smooth fest weekend, and a farewell dinner.

Tuckman's stageWhat it looks likeWhat helps
1 FormingMembers get acquainted; roles and goals are unclear.Clear goals and roles
2 StormingConflict, personality clashes, the leader challenged.Bring conflict into the open; agree how to work
3 NormingShared norms, roles accepted, trust growing.Reinforce the norms; step back a little
4 PerformingHigh efficiency, synergy, a self-managing team.Delegate, and protect the team from distraction
5 AdjourningThe task is complete; the team disbands and reflects.Recognise the work; record the lessons

Where it breaks. The stages describe a common pattern, not a law. Teams can skip a stage, slip back when a member changes, or storm and perform at the same time.

Forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.

blocks.title: Leadership
blocks.html:
Two managers take over two branches of the same bank. Same rules, same pay, same kind of customers. A year later one team is steady and the other has lost three people. What differed was how each one led.

In plain wordsLeadership is getting people to want to move in a direction, not only telling them to.

Exam definitionLeadership is the ability to influence a group toward the achievement of a vision or set of goals (Robbins and Judge).

A leader's core roles are to set direction, manage conflict, inspire and improve productivity. Thinking about how to do this has moved through four broad answers.

ApproachThe question it asksKey ideas
Trait (1930s–40s)Who makes a good leader?Drive, integrity, self-confidence, intelligence, knowledge of the business. No list of traits guarantees results.
Behavioural (1940s–60s)What do good leaders do?Lewin's three styles; the Ohio State studies (initiating structure and consideration); the Michigan studies (job-centred and employee-centred); Blake and Mouton's managerial grid
Contingency (1960s–70s)Which style suits which situation?Fiedler's contingency model; Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership; House's path–goal theory
Transformational (1970s onward)How do leaders change what followers want?Burns's transactional and transformational leadership; Bass's four Is; Greenleaf's servant leadership

Lewin's three styles (1939) are still the starting point:

StyleCore featureBest use and risk
AutocraticThe leader makes decisions aloneCrises and emergencies; fast, but overuse may demoralise
DemocraticMembers take part in decisionsBuilds participation and ownership; decisions may be slower
Laissez-faireHigh autonomy, minimal guidanceSkilled, self-motivated teams

Situational leadership turns the contingency idea into a practical rule: match the style to how ready the follower is for the task.

Transformational leaders change what followers want, not only what they do. Transactional leaders trade reward for effort. Verghese Kurien built Amul around an idea dairy farmers could own: a cooperative run by and for its milk producers. That is the transformational kind.

Effective leaders are visionary (future and strategic direction), empathetic (understand others' feelings), communicative (clear information and ideas), ethical (fair and morally sound decisions) and decisive (confident action).

Don't confuse leadership with management. In John Kotter's distinction, management copes with complexity: plans, budgets, control. Leadership copes with change: direction, alignment, motivation. Most managers need both.

Where it breaks. Style labels describe tendencies, not fixed types; most leaders shift between them. Trait lists read well but predict little on their own. Situational leadership is popular in training, but research gives it only mixed support.

For exams. Match each theory to its author and its key terms: LPC (Fiedler), readiness (Hersey and Blanchard), path–goal (House), the four Is (Bass), the grid (Blake and Mouton).

Go deeper for practitioners

Fiedler's contingency model (1967) treats style as fixed. A leader is task-motivated or relationship-motivated, measured by the least preferred co-worker (LPC) scale. A situation is more or less favourable depending on leader–member relations, task structure and position power. Task-motivated leaders do best when the situation is very favourable or very unfavourable; relationship-motivated leaders in between. The advice is to change the situation, or the leader, rather than the style.

House's path–goal theory (1971) says a leader's job is to clear the path to goals. It names four behaviours: directive, supportive, participative and achievement-oriented, chosen to fit the task and the people.

Blake and Mouton's grid (1964) plots concern for production against concern for people, each from 1 to 9: 1,1 impoverished; 9,1 authority–compliance; 1,9 country club; 5,5 middle of the road; 9,9 team management, the one they recommend.

Bass's four Is of transformational leadership: idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration. In Judge and Piccolo's 2004 review of many studies, both transformational leadership and contingent reward, a transactional behaviour, were strongly linked with followers' satisfaction and leaders' effectiveness; laissez-faire was linked with worse results.

A decision. A strong performer is promoted to lead her former peers. They are skilled and keen. Situational leadership says delegate; her instinct, wanting to prove herself, is to direct. Which costs more if she gets it wrong?

blocks.title: Group dynamics
blocks.html:
A board of capable people can still make a decision none of them would have made alone. Group dynamics explains how.

Group dynamics are the psychological processes and patterns of interaction at work within a group. They shape participation, collaboration, conflict resolution and performance.

  • Group size. Small groups allow deeper discussion and faster decisions. Large groups bring more diversity, but more coordination and communication problems.
  • Group cohesiveness is the degree of bonding and commitment among members. High cohesiveness improves coordination and performance; extreme cohesiveness may suppress dissent.
  • Groupthink happens when a group values harmony and avoiding conflict above critical evaluation: alternatives are ignored and decisions get worse. Irving Janis built the idea in 1972 from cases such as the Bay of Pigs invasion; Nixon's inner circle during Watergate is also often cited.

Signs of groupthink, in Janis's account: a feeling that the group cannot fail, explaining away warnings, pressure on anyone who disagrees, self-censorship, and an illusion that everyone agrees.

In practice. Ask someone to argue the other side, have the most senior person speak last, and bring in an outsider before a big decision.

Don't confuse cohesion with groupthink. Cohesion helps a group work together. Groupthink is what happens when keeping that cohesion matters more than getting the decision right.

Harmony above critical thinking: alternatives ignored, poor decisions.

text: The Gītā tells Arjuna to do the work that is his, because action is better than inaction. Social loafing is the opposite habit inside a group: holding back because others will cover. The verse speaks to one person's duty, not to group work, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Do your allotted work, for action is better than inaction.” नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः । niyataṃ kuru karma tvaṃ karma jyāyo hy akarmaṇaḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 3.8

pairings.classic: the crow that calls its kin
text: The Kuṟaḷ notes that a crow does not hide its food but calls its kin to share it, and says prosperity stays with people of that nature. Team building aims at the same habit: members who share rather than hoard. The couplet is about a ruler and his kin, so the comparison is offered for reflection.
pairings.quote: “The crow does not hide its food but calls its kin to eat; prosperity belongs to those of such nature.” காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் ஆக்கமும் அன்னநீ ரார்க்கே உள. Tirukkuṟaḷ 527

text: Tiruvaḷḷuvar names four qualities that should never fail in a ruler: fearlessness, generosity, wisdom and energy. They sit close to the traits listed for effective leaders, such as being decisive and visionary.
pairings.quote: “Fearlessness, generosity, wisdom and energy: never lacking these four is the nature of a ruler.” அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவூக்கம் இந்நான்கும் எஞ்சாமை வேந்தற் கியல்பு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 382

text: The Kuṟaḷ asks who could ruin a ruler who keeps advisers willing to rebuke him. Groupthink is the failure of that check: harmony is valued above critical evaluation, and the objections are never voiced.
pairings.quote: “Who can ruin the ruler who keeps advisers willing to rebuke him?” இடிக்குந் துணையாரை யாள்வாரை யாரே கெடுக்குந் தகைமை யவர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 447

pairings.classic: one who acts as he speaks
text: Tukaram says he will bow to the feet of whoever acts as he speaks. Leadership research finds credibility, doing what you say you will do, at the base of followers' trust. Tukaram is honouring a devotee, not describing a manager, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Whoever acts as he speaks, I will bow to his feet.” बोले तैसा चाले । त्याचीं वंदीन पाउलें ॥ bole taisā chāle, tyācīṃ vandīn pāuleṃ. Tukārām Gāthā 4291 (Marathi; Wikisource numbering)

chapters.title: Interpersonal Behaviour and Transactional Analysis
chapters.scope: How people communicate and respond to one another, the skills that make it work, and Eric Berne's transactional analysis.

blocks.title: Interpersonal behaviour and its patterns
blocks.html:
The manager of a public-sector bank branch snaps at a clerk at 10 a.m. By noon the clerk is curt with customers, and two of them complain. How people treat each other at work travels, and it travels both ways.

In plain wordsInterpersonal behaviour is how people talk to, listen to and react to one another.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: interpersonal behaviour is the way people communicate, respond and interact with one another, through verbal and non-verbal communication.

Words are only part of it. Non-verbal signals carry much of the message: tone of voice, body language, gestures and the emotions people show. A "fine" said with folded arms means something else. Interpersonal behaviour shapes teamwork, leadership, conflict resolution and, over time, the organisation's culture.

Four patterns. Who is talking to whom changes what the interaction needs. Take an auto-parts plant in Pune:

PatternCore ideaAt the plant
One-to-oneIndividual interaction; trust and clarity matter.A supervisor coaches one machine operator.
One-to-manyA leader communicates with a group; needs clarity and confidence.The plant head briefs the whole shift on a new safety rule.
Many-to-oneSeveral employees communicate with a superior; needs active listening.Operators bring a joint complaint about overtime to their supervisor.
Many-to-manyTeam interaction; needs collaboration, respect and openness.The shift team works out why rejects rose last week.

Reciprocal influence. A's behaviour influences B, and B's response in turn influences A. The loop can run up or down. Positive behaviour strengthens morale, motivation and cooperation; negative behaviour weakens them. In the bank branch, the clerk's curt replies make customers sharper, which makes the clerk sharper still.

Don't confuse interpersonal with intrapersonal. Intrapersonal processes happen inside one person: self-talk, one's own feelings and perception. Interpersonal behaviour happens between two or more people.

Where it breaks. The four patterns say who is talking to whom, not how well. A single meeting can move through all four in ten minutes. Reciprocal influence also explains why a bad exchange is hard to stop: each side waits for the other to soften first.

In practice. The quickest way to change a negative loop is to change your own response, since that is the half you control. Match the pattern to the message: give criticism one-to-one, and share a decision that affects everyone one-to-many, so all hear the same words.

For exams. Expect a question matching a pattern to what it needs, such as many-to-one with active listening.

blocks.title: Types, determinants and skills
blocks.html:
Two salespeople in an electronics showroom argue during a Diwali sale over who should serve a big customer. The same row can end in a clearer split of work, or in months of not speaking. What decides which?

In plain wordsPeople at work either pull together toward a shared goal, or pull apart because their goals or views differ.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: cooperative behaviour is working toward shared goals with mutual respect and openness; conflicting behaviour arises from differing goals, perceptions or misunderstandings.

TypeWhere it comes fromWhat it brings
CooperativeShared goals, respect and opennessTeamwork, creativity and collaboration
ConflictingDifferent goals, perceptions or misunderstandingsManaged constructively: role clarity, better understanding and innovative solutions

Back to the showroom. The manager hears both sides and splits the floor: one person takes televisions, the other kitchen appliances. The conflict produced role clarity. Ignored, it would have produced two people competing for every customer who walked in.

Six determinants shape how a person behaves toward others:

  • Personality: stable traits, such as being reserved or outgoing.
  • Perception: how a person reads others' actions. A late reply can look like rudeness or like a busy day.
  • Attitudes: settled feelings toward people, the job or the organisation.
  • Values: what a person thinks is right and important.
  • Emotional intelligence: the ability to recognise and manage one's own and others' emotions.
  • Motivation: what a person is trying to achieve in the exchange.

Five skills keep interaction constructive:

  • Positive thinking builds resilience and encourages constructive responses.
  • Mutual trust promotes transparency and open communication.
  • Empathy is understanding others' emotions and perspectives. It differs from sympathy, which is feeling sorry for someone.
  • Courtesy maintains respect and professional decorum.
  • Avoiding ego clashes supports harmony, cooperation and teamwork.

Don't confuse disagreement about the work with disagreement about each other. Conflict over tasks or methods, kept moderate, can improve decisions. Conflict over personalities rarely helps; it drains trust and attention. The showroom row became useful once it was about the floor, not about who was the better salesperson.

Where it breaks. The skills are easy to list and hard to practise under pressure. "Avoiding ego clashes" can slide into avoiding every disagreement, so problems stay hidden. The determinants also act together: a person with high emotional intelligence may still clash when their values are at stake.

For exams. Learn the six determinants and five skills as lists. A favourite statement to judge: "all conflict is harmful". It is false, because conflict managed constructively brings clarity and new solutions.

blocks.title: Transactional analysis: Johari window, ego states and transactions
blocks.html:
A team leader asks, "Has the report been sent?" and gets back, "Why are you always checking on me?" A plain question has turned into a quarrel. Transactional analysis explains how.

In plain wordsTransactional analysis looks at each exchange between two people and asks which part of each person spoke, and which part replied.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: transactional analysis (TA), developed by the psychiatrist Eric Berne, explains interactions through ego states, and is used to improve self-awareness, communication and relationships.

The Johari window is usually taught alongside TA as a map of self-awareness. Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham developed it; the name joins their first names. It sorts what is known about a person by two questions: do I know it, and do others know it?

Johari window areaKnown to selfKnown to othersWhat to do
OpenYesYesBuild trust and transparency
BlindNoYesReduce through feedback
HiddenYesNoReduce through self-disclosure
UnknownNoNoExplore through experience

The goal is to enlarge the open area, for better self-awareness, understanding and trust. A new branch manager who interrupts in meetings, without noticing, has it in her blind area. A colleague's honest word moves it into the open.

Ego states. Berne said each person speaks from one of three ego states, each a consistent set of thoughts, feelings and behaviour.

Ego stateWhat it holdsHow it shows
ParentValues, attitudes and behaviour learned from authority figuresGuiding or critical
AdultLogical, factual, rational processingObjective decisions
ChildEmotional, spontaneous, dependent responsesPlayful or rebellious

Transactions. A transaction is one message and its reply. In a complementary transaction the reply comes from the ego state the sender addressed, so communication flows. In a crossed transaction the reply comes from an unexpected ego state, causing misunderstanding or conflict. In an ulterior transaction two messages travel at once: an apparent social one and a hidden psychological one.

The team leader asked Adult to Adult. "Yes, at four o'clock" would have been complementary. "Why are you always checking on me?" came from the Child, aimed at a Parent the leader never used: a crossed transaction.

Don't confuse the two models. The Johari window comes from Luft and Ingham, not from Berne; it is taught with TA because both aim at self-awareness. And an ego state is not an age or a family role: a 25-year-old can speak from the Parent, and a grandparent from the Child.

Where it breaks. TA grew out of clinical practice rather than controlled research, so its terms are easier to use than to test. Labelling a colleague's reply "Child" can also become a way of dismissing them.

For exams. Expect: which Johari area shrinks through feedback (blind) and which through self-disclosure (hidden); and naming a transaction from a short dialogue.

Go deeper for practitioners

Finer states. TA writers often split the Parent into a Nurturing Parent and a Critical (or Controlling) Parent, and the Child into a Free (or Natural) Child and an Adapted Child. "Take a break, you look tired" is Nurturing Parent; "This is careless work" is Critical Parent.

A decision. Your plant sends a circular: "All staff must strictly ensure timely submission of overtime forms. Repeated lapses will not be tolerated." Submissions fall further, and the union protests. The circular spoke from the Critical Parent and drew an Adapted or rebellious Child reply. An Adult version gives the fact, the reason and the fix: "Forms after Friday miss the payroll run, so overtime is paid a month late. Here is the new drop box." Which version would you send?

Links. The blind area is the case for upward and peer feedback in performance appraisal. Perception, in the personality chapter of this unit, explains why the same words land differently on different people.

blocks.title: Life scripts, life positions, strokes and games
blocks.html:
One officer in a district office meets every new idea with "that won't work here". Another keeps rescuing a junior who never learns. Transactional analysis says such habits follow from how people see themselves and others.

In plain wordsA life script is the story about yourself that you learned as a child and still act out without noticing.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a life script is a largely unconscious pattern formed in childhood that shapes later decisions, relationships and behaviour.

TA aims to recognise unhelpful patterns, change behaviour and support personal growth. Four tools describe the patterns: life positions, strokes, games and the script itself.

Life positions are a person's basic stance toward self and others. Thomas Harris's book I'm OK – You're OK made the phrase widely known.

Life positionOrientationResultSounds like
I'm OK, you're OKPositive toward self and othersHealthy relationships: the ideal position"Let's work it out together."
I'm OK, you're not OKSuperior, blamingTension and conflict"If they did their jobs, we'd be fine."
I'm not OK, you're OKInferior, submissiveDependency"You decide, you know better."
I'm not OK, you're not OKNegative toward self and othersDisengagement"Nothing here will ever change."

Strokes. A stroke is an act of recognition: a word, a nod, a note. Positive strokes (praise, appreciation) build morale and motivation; negative strokes (criticism, disapproval) may discourage. TA also separates conditional strokes, for what a person does, from unconditional strokes, for who they are. People who get no positive strokes may seek negative ones, since being noticed beats being ignored. Managers should give genuine, specific recognition.

Example. A supervisor in a Nashik packing unit says, "Your line had zero rejects this week, and I noticed you trained the newcomer too." That is a positive, conditional stroke, and it tells the worker exactly what to repeat.

Games. Games are recurring patterns of interaction with hidden motives that lead to predictable, often unhelpful outcomes. Eric Berne described many in Games People Play. In "Yes, but…", a person asks for solutions and then rejects each one: "Yes, but we have no budget." "Yes, but the boss won't agree." The hidden aim is to avoid responsibility, and both sides end up frustrated.

Don't confuse a game with one ulterior transaction. An ulterior transaction is a single exchange with a hidden message. A game is a chain of such exchanges, repeated over time, that ends in the same bad feeling. And in TA a game is not play: nobody enjoys the ending.

Where it breaks. Life positions are a counselling vocabulary, not measured traits; one person can shift position from one setting to another. Naming a colleague's "game" aloud usually makes them defensive rather than aware.

In practice. To stop "Yes, but…", stop supplying answers. Ask, "What would you suggest?" This hands back responsibility. To build an OK–OK climate, make strokes specific and frequent, and criticise the work, not the person.

I'm OK, you're OK.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says friendship is not for laughing together but for stepping in to rebuke a friend who goes wrong. In Johari's terms, a friend's honest feedback shrinks the blind area: what others can see in us that we cannot.
pairings.quote: “Friendship is not for laughing together; it is for stepping in to rebuke when one goes too far.” நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென் றிடித்தற் பொருட்டு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 784

text: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad pictures the self as a rider in a chariot: the body is the chariot, the intellect the charioteer and the mind the reins. A modern reader may see the Adult ego state as the charioteer, steering learned habit and raw feeling. The Upaniṣad describes the self's journey, so this is a reading, not Berne's model.
pairings.quote: “Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins.” आत्मानं रथिनं विद्धि शरीरं रथमेव तु । बुद्धिं तु सारथिं विद्धि मनः प्रग्रहमेव च । ātmānaṃ rathinaṃ viddhi śarīraṃ ratham eva tu, buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi manaḥ pragraham eva ca. Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3

text: Kabir advises keeping a critic close, even housing him in your courtyard, because he cleans your nature without soap or water. The Johari window says the blind area, what others see in us and we do not, shrinks only through feedback. Both treat criticism from others as the way to see yourself.
pairings.quote: “Keep your critic close; give him a hut in your courtyard. Without water, without soap, he makes your nature clean.” निन्दक नियरे राखिये, आंगन कुटी छवाय । बिन पानी साबुन बिना, निरमल करे सुभाय ॥ nindak niyare rākhiye, āṅgan kuṭī chhavāy; bin pānī sābun binā, nirmal kare subhāy. Kabīr, sākhī (Hindi)

chapters.title: Organisational Culture and Climate
chapters.scope: The shared meaning that makes one organisation unlike another, how it is built and kept, and how it feels to work there.

blocks.title: What organisational culture is
blocks.html:
Two private banks in the same city sell the same products at similar rates. In one, a clerk who spots an error tells the manager at once; in the other, she keeps quiet. No rule book explains the difference.

In plain wordsCulture is "the way we do things here": the values and habits people in an organisation share, often without saying them.

Exam definitionOrganisational culture is a system of shared meaning held by members that distinguishes the organisation from other organisations (Robbins and Judge).

Culture is made of shared values, beliefs and norms. It shapes how things are done there, and new members pick it up mostly by watching.

Three levels. Edgar Schein showed that culture sits at different depths. What you can see on a visit is only the top layer.

In the first bank, the artefact might be an "error of the week" board. The espoused value is "we own our mistakes". The basic assumption, never written down, is that reporting an error will not cost you your job. That last layer is why the clerk speaks up.

Seven characteristics. Robbins and Judge list seven characteristics that, taken together, capture an organisation's culture. Each runs from low to high, so a culture is a profile across all seven.

DimensionWhat it measures
Innovation and risk-takingExperimentation, creativity, willingness to take risks
Attention to detailPrecision, analysis, thoroughness
Outcome orientationResults, performance, achieving targets
People orientationThe effect of decisions on employees and their well-being
Team orientationCollaboration and collective achievement
AggressivenessCompetitiveness and assertiveness
StabilityOrder, consistency, keeping the status quo

For illustration: a young software firm in Bengaluru might score high on innovation and outcomes and low on stability. A long-established insurance office might show the reverse profile. Neither is wrong; each fits different work.

Don't confuse culture with the rule book. Policies are written and official. Culture is what people actually do. When the two disagree, people usually follow the culture.

Where it breaks. The seven characteristics describe a culture; they do not say which culture is best. That depends on the work and the strategy. Culture is also hard to measure: surveys pick up espoused values far more easily than the assumptions underneath.

For exams. Learn the Robbins and Judge definition word for word, the seven characteristics, and Schein's three levels in order: artefacts, espoused values, basic assumptions.

blocks.title: Strength and functions of culture
blocks.html:
In a family-run chain of sweet shops, every new hire hears the founder's rule on day one: never sell yesterday's sweets. Years later, staff still throw out unsold stock with no manager watching. That is what a strong culture looks like.

In plain wordsA culture is strong when most people hold the same core values, and hold them firmly.

Exam definitionIn a strong culture, the organisation's core values are both intensely held and widely shared (Robbins and Judge).
