chapters.title: Human Resource Management
chapters.scope: What HRM is, how it grew, what it aims at and does, and how it differs from personnel management and from organisational behaviour.

blocks.title: Meaning and objectives of HRM
blocks.html:
An auto-parts plant in Pune can buy a new machine and have it running within weeks. Finding, training and keeping the people who run it well takes far longer, and fails more often. That slower job is human resource management.

In plain wordsHRM is everything an organisation does to find, grow, motivate and keep the people it needs.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: HRM is the process of acquiring, developing, motivating and retaining employees to achieve organisational goals. Gary Dessler's version: the process of acquiring, training, appraising and compensating employees, and of attending to their labour relations, health and safety, and fairness concerns.

Acquire → Develop → Motivate → Retain: a skilled, motivated and committed workforce

At the Pune plant, an illustration. It acquires twelve machine operators through an industrial training institute and a referral drive. It develops them with a month of training on the new machine. It motivates them with a shift allowance and public recognition for zero-defect weeks. It retains them with a clear path to supervisor.

HRM aims to maximise performance, ensure employee welfare and align people with the organisation's strategy. Its objectives fall into three groups.

ObjectivesWhose interestExamples
PersonalThe employeeTraining, career development, work-life balance, satisfaction
OrganisationalThe organisationProductivity, performance, workforce planning, talent management
OtherSociety and the lawLegal compliance, social responsibility, diversity and inclusion, fairness

The same three-way split appears in Edwin Flippo's classic definition of personnel management, which ends: so that individual, organisational and societal objectives are accomplished.

Don't confuse HRM with the HR department. Every manager who hires, coaches, appraises or disciplines is doing HRM. The HR department designs the systems and supports managers; it cannot do their people work for them.

Where it breaks. The objectives can pull against each other. Long overtime raises output but hurts work-life balance; cutting pay costs helps the budget but strains welfare and retention. HRM has to choose, and the definitions do not say how.

For exams. Learn one definition well, the four verbs (acquire, develop, motivate, retain) and the three groups of objectives with an example of each.

blocks.title: Evolution of HRM
blocks.html:
A modern HR team talks about analytics and engagement. A nineteenth-century factory had a foreman with a book of fines. The change came in stages, and each stage left behind something HR still does.

The eight stages fall into three broad shifts: from controlling workers, to caring about them as people, to treating them as part of strategy.

StagePeriodFocus
Pre-industrialBefore the 18th centuryAgrarian and manual work; no formal HR
Industrial Revolution18th–19th centuryFactory system, supervision, discipline, productivity
Scientific managementLate 19th–early 20th centuryF. W. Taylor: efficiency, time and motion, standardisation
Human relations1920s–1930sElton Mayo: social factors, morale, motivation
Post-war personnel1940s–1950sPersonnel departments, hiring, training, labour relations
Modern HRM1960s–1980sFrom personnel administration to HR development and motivation
TQM and globalisation1980s–1990sQuality, employee involvement, continuous improvement
Strategic HRM2000s onwardHR information systems, analytics, diversity, a global workforce, strategic alignment

What each stage left behind. Taylor's The Principles of Scientific Management (1911) left work measurement and standard methods. Elton Mayo's reading of the Hawthorne studies at Western Electric (1924–1932) left the idea that morale and the work group affect output. The personnel era left the HR department, with its hiring, training and labour relations. Strategic HRM adds data and a seat in business planning.

Don't confuse the human relations stage with HRM. The human relations movement of the 1920s and 1930s was about social needs and morale. HRM came decades later and is broader: it covers planning, development, reward and strategy as one system.

Where it breaks. The stages are a teaching device, not a strict timeline. Many small firms still run HR at the personnel stage, and scientific management's methods are alive in every call centre that times its calls.

For exams. Expect to match a stage with its period, person or focus: Taylor with efficiency, Mayo with morale, the 2000s with analytics and strategic alignment.

Control, efficiency, human relations, personnel, HRM, strategic HR.

blocks.title: Functions of HRM
blocks.html:
The owner of a growing kirana chain opens her fifth store and finds she spends half her week on staff. She is hiring, training, settling pay, calming a quarrel and arranging care for an injured helper. Each of those is one function of HRM.

HRM is carried out through eight functions. Together they follow an employee from before hiring to the next generation of leaders.

FunctionActivityPurposeAt the kirana chain (an illustration)
PlanHuman resource planningForecast manpower requirementsTwo more counter staff for each new store
AcquireRecruitment and selectionAttract and select suitable employeesReferrals from current staff; a short trial day
DevelopTraining and developmentBuild knowledge, skills and capabilitiesTeach the billing software and stock rotation
EvaluatePerformance appraisalAssess performance and find areas to improveA monthly review of billing errors and customer complaints
RewardCompensation managementFair pay, benefits and retentionSalary plus a Diwali bonus tied to the store's sales
RelateEmployee relationsCommunication, cooperation and conflict resolutionA weekly meeting where staff raise problems
ProtectSafety and welfareHealth, safety and well-beingSafe stacking of heavy sacks; a first-aid kit; insurance
PrepareCareer and succession planningFuture talent and leadership continuityTrain a senior helper to run the next store

Don't confuse operative functions with managerial functions. In Edwin Flippo's classic split, the managerial functions of HR are planning, organising, directing and controlling. The operative functions are procurement, development, compensation, integration, maintenance and separation. The eight functions above are operative ones in modern names.

Where it breaks. The functions overlap: appraisal feeds both reward and training. In a small firm one person does all eight, and some, like payroll, are often outsourced.

For exams. Expect "which function does this activity belong to?" Performance appraisal is evaluate; compensation is reward; safety and welfare is protect; succession planning is prepare.

blocks.title: Approaches to HRM, and how HRM differs
blocks.html:
Two firms both say they "do HR". One keeps neat files and pays on time. The other asks which skills it will need to win in five years, and hires and trains for them now. They are following different approaches.

In plain wordsStrategic HRM means planning people decisions around where the business is going, not only around today's paperwork.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: strategic HRM links HR policies and practices with the organisation's strategic goals in order to improve business performance.

The ten approaches below run roughly from the oldest view (people as records to administer) to the newest (people as a source of advantage, managed with evidence).

ApproachCore idea
TraditionalAdministrative control, records, compliance
Human relationsMotivation, morale and social needs
Human resource developmentLearning, skills and career development
ContingencyHR practices depend on the situation; no single best way
Strategic HRMHR strategy aligned with business strategy
High-performance work systemsTeamwork, empowerment and performance-linked rewards
Best practicesSome HR practices improve performance almost everywhere
Resource-based viewPeople as strategic resources for lasting competitive advantage
Employee-centricWell-being, engagement, flexibility and inclusion
Evidence-basedData and evidence guide HR decisions

Three that answer the same question differently. Is there one right way to manage people? Best practices says yes, some practices work almost everywhere. Contingency (also called best fit) says no, it depends on the firm's situation and strategy. The resource-based view, from Jay Barney (1991), says advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and hard to substitute. A skilled, loyal workforce can be such a resource, because a rival cannot buy it overnight.

HRM against personnel management.

BasisHRMPersonnel management
PhilosophyStrategic and proactiveAdministrative and reactive
FocusPeople and business strategyRoutine employee administration
ScopeBroad: development, engagement, planningNarrow: payroll, records, compliance
Employee relationsParticipation and engagementControl and grievance handling
DevelopmentLearning, potential and growthMainly task-specific training

Don't confuse HRM with organisational behaviour. Organisational behaviour (OB) studies why people act as they do at work: motivation, perception, groups. HRM uses that knowledge to design hiring, pay and training. OB explains; HRM acts.

Where it breaks. Critics such as Karen Legge argued that the contrast between HRM and personnel management lies more in the language than in practice. Many "HR" departments still mostly run payroll and compliance. Best practices and best fit each have supporting studies, and neither has won the argument.

For exams. Match each approach to its core idea, especially contingency against best practices and the resource-based view. Learn the HRM–personnel table row by row.

Go deeper for practitioners

Hard and soft HRM. The Michigan model (Fombrun, Tichy and Devanna, 1984) is the classic "hard" view: people are a resource to be fitted to strategy and managed for performance. The Harvard model (Beer and colleagues, 1984) is the classic "soft" view: it starts from stakeholders and aims at commitment, competence and long-term well-being.

Best practices in one list. Jeffrey Pfeffer (1998) named seven practices: employment security, selective hiring, self-managed teams, high pay tied to performance, extensive training, fewer status differences, and sharing information.

What HR people do. Dave Ulrich (1997) described four roles for HR: strategic partner, administrative expert, employee champion and change agent. A department that plays only the administrative role is personnel management under a new name.

A decision. A 60-person software firm in Kochi loses its best engineers to larger rivals. A best-practice answer copies the big firms' benefits. A best-fit answer asks what a small firm can offer that they cannot: faster responsibility, visible impact, flexible hours. The resource-based question is which skills the firm must keep in-house at any cost.

Links. Strategic HRM (this unit) takes these models further.

HRM asks “How do we manage people?”; organisational behaviour asks “Why do people behave the way they do?”

text: The Kuṟaḷ's rule for assigning work: having judged that this person will accomplish this task by these means, leave the task to them. Acquiring and developing a workforce turns that judgement into a system.
pairings.quote: “Having judged that this person can accomplish this task by these means, entrust the task to them.” இதனை இதனால் இவன்முடிக்கும் என்றாய்ந் ததனை அவன்கண் விடல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 517

chapters.title: Human Resource Planning
chapters.scope: Forecasting and balancing the demand for and supply of people, so the right people are in the right place at the right time.

blocks.title: Meaning of human resource planning
blocks.html:
An auto-parts plant in Pune wins an export order that needs a second shift from April. If it starts hiring in March, the new line stands idle. If it hires a year early, it pays wages for months of no work.

In plain wordsHuman resource planning (HRP) is working out how many people, with which skills, the organisation will need, and how it will have them in time.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: HRP is the process of forecasting and managing the demand for and supply of human resources, so that the organisation has the right people, in the right place, at the right time. An older definition, usually credited to E. W. Vetter, calls it the process by which management determines how an organisation should move from its current manpower position to its desired manpower position.

HRP compares two forecasts. Demand is the number and kind of people the organisation will need. Supply is the number and kind it will actually have. Its core objective is balance between the two: the human resources available and what the organisation requires.

Result of the comparisonWhat it meansTypical actions
ShortageDemand is greater than supplyRecruit; train or promote people inside; overtime; temporary or contract staff
SurplusSupply is greater than demandFreeze hiring; retrain and redeploy; reduce hours; voluntary retirement schemes
BalanceDemand and supply matchReplace leavers; keep watching the forecasts

At the Pune plant, an illustration. The second shift needs 40 more operators by 1 April. Hiring them from industrial training institutes takes about three months, and they then need a month of training. Working backwards, the plant must start recruiting by early December and train in March.

A shortage costs lost orders and overtime. A surplus costs wages for idle people. HRP treats both as planning failures.

Don't confuse HRP with recruitment. HRP decides how many people of which kind are needed, and when. Recruitment comes after it and goes out to find them, and only for the gap that cannot be filled from inside.

Where it breaks. Every HRP figure rests on a forecast of the business: sales, technology and how many people will leave. A cancelled order or a new machine can overturn it. That is why plans are reviewed regularly, and often drawn up for more than one possible future.

For exams. Learn the phrase "the right number and the right kind of people, at the right place, at the right time"; the two sides, demand and supply; and balance as the objective. HRP comes first in staffing: recruitment, selection and training follow from it.

blocks.title: The HRP process
blocks.html:
A plan that starts by counting vacancies only replaces the people who left. A plan that starts from the business strategy also prepares for the work that is coming.

The HRP process runs in eight steps, from the organisation's goals to a regular review. In short: strategy, forecast, analyse, match, act, review.

StepWhat it involves
1 Analyse organisational objectivesUnderstand the mission, strategy and future business goals
2 Forecast HR demandEstimate future workforce needs from expansion, technology and production
3 Analyse HR supplyAssess available talent, skills, turnover, promotions and succession
4 Identify skill gapsCompare existing skills with those required
5 Determine workforce requirementsThe number and type of employees needed, by department
6 Match demand and supplyFind shortages or surpluses
7 Develop HR action plansRecruitment, training, redeployment, retention
8 Monitor and controlTrack measures, review outcomes, update plans as conditions change

The arithmetic at the heart of steps 2 to 6 is simple:

Forecast supply = present staff − expected leavers − promotions and transfers out + promotions and transfers in
Net requirement = forecast demand − forecast supply

A worked example, with illustrative numbers. The Pune plant has 100 machine operators. Its business plan raises output by 20% next year, with no change in output per operator.

  1. Demand (step 2): 100 × 1.2 = 120 operators.
  2. Supply (step 3): records show about 10% of operators leave each year, so about 10 will go. Four will be promoted to supervisor. Supply at year-end: 100 − 10 − 4 = 86.
  3. Gap (steps 4 to 6): 120 − 86 = 34 operators short.
  4. Action (step 7): retrain 4 people from the packing section, which needs fewer hands after automation, and recruit 30 through industrial training institutes. 4 + 30 = 34.
  5. Review (step 8): check every quarter. If more than 10 operators leave, raise the hiring target.

Don't confuse forecasting demand with analysing supply. Demand asks how many people the work will need. Supply asks how many of the right people the organisation will actually have, after exits and internal moves.

Where it breaks. The steps look like a straight line, but real planning loops back. A gap too large to fill may send managers back to change the business plan itself. The numbers are also only as good as the records behind them.

For exams. Expect questions on the order of the steps, and on which step a given activity belongs to. Action plans come only after demand and supply have been matched.

Go deeper for practitioners

How demand is forecast. Textbooks list several methods, often used together.

  • Managerial judgement: managers estimate needs from experience, either bottom-up from departments or top-down from senior management.
  • Delphi technique: experts give estimates anonymously in rounds. A facilitator summarises each round, and the experts revise until their views converge.
  • Trend analysis: past staffing levels are projected forward, usually against a business factor such as sales.
  • Ratio analysis: a ratio between a business factor and staff is applied to the forecast. An illustration: a bank branch has one teller for every 1,000 savings accounts. If accounts grow from 6,000 to 8,000, it needs 8 tellers instead of 6.
  • Work-study: the hours a task needs are worked out from time standards, then divided by the hours one person works. An illustration: 60,000 units at 0.5 hours each is 30,000 hours. At 2,000 working hours a year per operator, that is 30,000 ÷ 2,000 = 15 operators.

Links. Supply analysis, the next block, covers step 3 in detail. Recruitment and selection, and training and development, are the main action plans of step 7.

Strategy, forecast, analyse, match, act, review.

blocks.title: Methods of supply analysis
blocks.html:
The Pune plant knows it needs 34 more operators. Before it advertises, it should ask two questions. Who inside could fill some of these posts, and how many of today's staff will still be there next year?

In plain wordsSupply analysis takes stock of the people the organisation has, and works out how that will change by the date of the plan.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: supply forecasting estimates the number and kind of people who will be available at a future date, from within the organisation and from the outside labour market.

Six methods look at the people already there: their skills, their potential, and how they move and leave.

MethodLooks atAt the Pune plant (an illustration)
Skills inventoryEmployees' qualifications, skills and experienceA record shows which operators can already set up the new machines
Succession planningPotential future leaders for critical positionsTwo named successors for the plant head, each with a development plan
Turnover analysisExit patterns and what they mean for future staffingMost leavers quit within their first year
Promotion and mobility analysisInternal movement and advancement potentialFour operators are ready to become supervisors
Job analysisDuties, responsibilities and required competenciesThe new line's operators must read technical drawings
Scenario planningPossible future situations and their workforce implicationsStaffing if the export order doubles, and if it is cancelled

Turnover in numbers. The usual measure is the labour turnover rate:

Labour turnover rate = separations during the period ÷ average number of employees × 100

An illustration: a department starts the year with 95 people and ends it with 105, and 12 people leave during the year. Average staff = (95 + 105) ÷ 2 = 100. Turnover = 12 ÷ 100 × 100 = 12%.

Looking outside. The six methods look inside the organisation. Supply analysis also looks at the outside labour market. For the Pune plant, that means how many trained machinists local institutes produce each year, and what nearby plants pay them.

Don't confuse a skills inventory with job analysis. A skills inventory describes people: what each employee can do. Job analysis describes jobs: what each job needs. HRP compares the two to find skill gaps.

Where it breaks. Records go stale: a skills inventory updated once in five years misses new skills and recent leavers. Past turnover may not repeat if a rival plant opens next door. Succession plans can favour people who resemble today's leaders.

In practice. Turnover analysis is most useful broken down: by department, by length of service and by reason for leaving. A high rate among first-year joiners points to hiring or induction, not pay alone.

Go deeper for practitioners

Markov analysis projects internal supply from past rates of movement between jobs, set out in a transition matrix. An illustration for a smaller section of the plant:

NowStay in the jobPromotedLeave
40 operators80%: 3210%: 4 become supervisors10%: 4
10 supervisors90%: 9none in this example10%: 1

Next year's internal supply is 32 operators and 9 + 4 = 13 supervisors. If the section still needs 40 operators and 10 supervisors, it must hire 8 operators, and it will have 3 supervisors more than it needs unless it plans for them.

Replacement charts are the simple form of succession planning. For each key post they show the likely successors, how ready each one is, and how well each performs now.

A decision. Turnover analysis shows that 60% of leavers go within their first year. Do you raise starting pay, or fix how new joiners are selected and inducted? The breakdown by reason for leaving should decide, not the overall rate.

pairings.modern: Right person, right work, right time
pairings.classic: the doer, the work and the time
text: The Kuṟaḷ advises acting only after weighing the doer, the work and the right time together. Human resource planning asks a workforce the same three questions: who, for what work, and when.
pairings.quote: “Weigh the doer, weigh the work, and act knowing the right time.” செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 516

chapters.title: Recruitment and Selection
chapters.scope: Attracting a pool of suitable candidates, then choosing the best of them: the sources, the steps and the tests.

blocks.title: Recruitment and its sources
blocks.html:
A private bank needs a manager for its Lucknow branch. It can promote its best assistant manager, whom everyone knows. Or it can hire someone from a rival bank who has run a larger branch. Inside or outside is the first question of recruitment.

In plain wordsRecruitment is getting enough suitable people to apply for a job.

Exam definitionRecruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs in the organisation (Edwin Flippo). A fuller textbook version: searching for, identifying and attracting qualified candidates, to build a pool of capable candidates for current and future needs.

Vacancy → attract candidates → talent pool → selection

Recruitment draws on two kinds of source. Internal sources look inside the organisation:

Internal methodKey focus
Job postingAnnouncing the vacancy internally
Employee referralsRecommendations by employees
PromotionsMovement to higher positions
TransfersMovement across departments or locations
Rehiring retired employeesPart-time or project engagement
Previous applicantsReconsidering earlier applicants

External sources look outside: online recruitment, social media, recruitment agencies, job fairs, campus recruitment, headhunting, internships, walk-ins, temporary or contract hiring, poaching and government job centres. Headhunting means a search firm approaches people who are not looking for a job. Poaching means hiring people away from a competitor. A walk-in is an open interview day that anyone eligible can attend.

SourceAdvantagesDrawbacks
InternalCosts less; faster; lifts morale; supports career development; the person is already knownA small pool; few new ideas; each promotion leaves another vacancy; those passed over may resent it
ExternalA wider talent pool; fresh skills; new perspectives and innovationCosts more; takes longer; the newcomer is less known, so the risk of a bad hire is higher; insiders may feel overlooked

Back at the bank. Promoting the assistant manager is quick and rewards loyalty, but then the bank needs a new assistant manager. Hiring from the rival brings experience of a larger branch, at a higher salary and with more risk.

Don't confuse an internal source with an internal candidate. Employee referrals count as an internal method because they work through current staff. The people referred, though, usually come from outside.

Where it breaks. Neither source is better in general. Heavy internal hiring can make an organisation inward-looking. Heavy reliance on referrals can make a workforce less diverse, because people tend to refer people like themselves.

For exams. Expect to classify a source as internal or external, and to give two advantages of each.

blocks.title: The recruitment process
blocks.html:
A company advertises "Sales executive wanted" and gets 2,000 applications, almost none of them suitable. The fault lies in the steps before the advertisement, not in the advertisement itself.

Recruitment runs from recognising a staffing need to checking how well the hiring went. In short: need, analyse, attract, screen, build, evaluate.

StepPurpose
1 Identify the vacancyRecognise the staffing need
2 Job analysisDetermine duties and required skills
3 Job description and specificationDefine responsibilities and qualifications
4 Advertise the jobUse internal and external channels
5 Receive and review applicationsScreen and shortlist
6 Build a talent poolKeep potential candidates in view
7 Employer brandingAttract quality applicants
8 Initial communicationGive role clarity
9 NetworkingReach passive candidates
10 Recruitment campaignsPlan hiring drives
11 Tracking and reportingEvaluate how well recruitment worked

A passive candidate is someone good who is not looking for a job, so never sees an advertisement. Employer branding is the organisation's reputation as a place to work.

Tracking in numbers (step 11). A yield ratio compares the number of candidates at one stage with the number who reach the next. An illustration: a consumer-goods firm hires sales executives in Indore.

Next year the firm needs 12 people. Working backwards with the same ratios: 12 ÷ 0.8 = 15 offers; 15 × 4 = 60 interviews; 60 × 7.5 = 450 applications. If the drive cost ₹2.4 lakh for the 8 hires, the cost per hire was ₹2,40,000 ÷ 8 = ₹30,000.

Don't confuse the job description with the job specification. The description sets out the job: its duties and responsibilities. The specification sets out the person: the qualifications, skills and experience needed. The 2,000 unsuitable applications usually trace back to a vague specification.

Where it breaks. The steps are not a strict sequence. Branding, networking and the talent pool run all the time, not once per vacancy. A large number of applications is also a poor goal in itself: every unsuitable one costs screening time.

In practice. Common measures for step 11 are time to fill a post, cost per hire, source of hire, offer acceptance rate, and quality of hire, often judged by the new person's first appraisal.

For exams. Expect the order of the first steps (vacancy, job analysis, description and specification, then advertising) and the purpose of a named step.

Need, analyse, attract, screen, build, evaluate.

blocks.title: Selection and selection tests
blocks.html:
Fifty people apply for one post of assistant at a cooperative bank. Interviewing each of them for an hour would take fifty hours. Selection removes the unsuitable step by step, with the cheapest checks first.

In plain wordsSelection is choosing, from the people who applied, the one who best fits the job and the organisation.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: selection is the process of evaluating applicants and choosing the most suitable candidate from the applicant pool. Its goal is to match the candidate's skills, attitude and values with the organisation's requirements.

Application review → preliminary screening → shortlisting → interview → tests → verification → medical → offer → onboarding

Each step is a hurdle: a candidate who fails it goes no further. Early hurdles are cheap and remove many people. Later ones are costly and are kept for a few. Some organisations hold tests before the interview to shorten the interview list; the order in the line above is one common version.

Selection testMeasuresAn illustration
Intelligence testReasoning, analysis and problem-solvingNumber series and logical puzzles for management trainees
Aptitude testAbility to learn job-specific skillsA test of logical thinking for trainees who will learn programming
Interest testOccupational preferencesA questionnaire on whether a person prefers working with people, data or machines
Personality testBehaviour and emotional stabilityHow a candidate for a call centre handles pressure and angry customers
Achievement testJob-related knowledge and proficiencyAn accounts test for an experienced accountant
Trade testTechnical, job-specific abilityAn electrician wires a small panel
Dexterity testManual skill and coordinationFitting small parts onto a circuit board against the clock

What makes a test worth using. It must be reliable: it gives consistent results when the same person takes it again. It must also be valid: its scores predict how well people do the job. A typing-speed test is valid for a data-entry post, not for a sales post.

Don't confuse an aptitude test with an achievement test. Aptitude is potential: how well a person could learn the skill. Achievement is what the person has already learnt. Use aptitude tests for freshers and achievement tests for experienced hires.

Where it breaks. Interviews, especially unplanned ones, invite bias: a strong first impression, or liking people similar to oneself. Candidates can fake answers on personality questionnaires. A written test in English can screen out able candidates whose English is weaker, when the job does not need it.

For exams. Match each test to what it measures, and know the order of the selection steps.

Go deeper for practitioners

What the research shows. Frank Schmidt and John Hunter's 1998 review combined decades of studies on how well selection methods predict job performance. General mental ability tests, work-sample tests and structured interviews were among the best single predictors. Unstructured interviews did less well, and years of experience predicted little. A 2022 re-analysis by Paul Sackett and colleagues lowered many of these estimates and placed structured interviews at the top.

A structured interview asks every candidate the same job-related questions and scores the answers against a written guide. Many questions ask for past behaviour: "Tell us about a time a customer complained. What did you do?"

A decision. A branch manager wants to hire the candidate she "clicked with" in a twenty-minute chat. The candidate scored lowest on the structured interview panel. Which evidence should carry more weight, and how would you explain the choice to her?

blocks.title: Recruitment against selection
blocks.html:
A college placement cell reports that 900 students applied to one company, and the company hired 12. The 900 is the result of recruitment. The 12 is the result of selection.

The two are consecutive stages of hiring. Recruitment widens the pool; selection narrows it to the people who will be hired.

BasisRecruitmentSelection
MeaningAttracting potential candidatesChoosing the best candidate
ObjectiveCreate an applicant poolIdentify the suitable candidate
NaturePositive: encourages applicantsNegative: eliminates unsuitable applicants
ScopeBroad: sourcing and attractingNarrow: screening and evaluation
OutcomeA pool of candidatesThe final hiring decision
ResponsibilityMainly the HR recruitment teamHR with departmental heads

At the placement drive. Recruitment was the company's campus talk, its advertisement and its reputation, which brought 900 applications. Selection was the aptitude test, the group discussion and the interviews, which rejected 888 of them.

Don't read "negative" as "bad". Selection is called negative because it rejects far more people than it accepts. Recruitment is positive because it invites people in. Both are needed.

Where it breaks. The line between them is not sharp. Screening and shortlisting appear in both lists: as step 5 of recruitment and as the early steps of selection. In practice the same HR team often does both.

In practice. A recruiter judged only on the number of applications floods the selectors with unsuitable people. Judge recruitment by the quality of the pool, and selection by how the hires perform.

For exams. The table is a favourite: positive against negative, pool against decision, broad against narrow.

Recruitment attracts, for more candidates; selection chooses, for the best candidate.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says a person should be chosen after being tested on four things: virtue, wealth, pleasure and the fear of losing life. Modern selection tests ability, aptitude and personality; the couplet tests character under temptation and threat.
pairings.quote: “Choose a person after testing them in four ways: by virtue, by wealth, by pleasure and by the fear of death.” அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம் நான்கின் திறந்தெரிந்து தேறப் படும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 501

text: Kauṭilya tells the ruler to test ministers in secret through four trials (upadhā), of righteousness, wealth, desire and fear, and to place each in work that suits what the trials showed. The home page's sample concept compares this with modern selection; secret trials of this kind would breach today's ethics and employment law.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 1.10

text: The Kuṟaḷ warns that trusting someone who has not been tested, and doubting someone who has, both bring endless trouble. It is the case for a careful selection process, and for trusting its result once it is done.
pairings.quote: “To trust the untested, and to doubt the one you have tested, both bring endless sorrow.” தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும் தீரா இடும்பை தரும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 510

text: Vemana notes that salt and camphor look alike, and only tasting shows the difference; so too among people. Selection tests exist for the same reason: applicants who look alike on paper differ once their abilities are tried. Vemana is speaking of character in general, so this is a reading.

Listen, Vema.” ఉప్పు కప్పురంబు ఒక్క పోలికనుండు, చూడ చూడ రుచుల జాడ వేరు, పురుషులందు పుణ్యపురుషులు వేరయా, విశ్వదాభిరామ వినుర వేమ uppu kappurambu okka pōlikanuṇḍu, chūḍa chūḍa ruchula jāḍa vēru, puruṣulandu puṇyapuruṣulu vērayā, viśvadābhirāma vinura vēma. Vēmana, padyam (Telugu)

chapters.title: Training and Development
chapters.scope: Building skills for today's job and growing people for tomorrow's: the methods, the process and the difference between the two.

blocks.title: Training and its methods
blocks.html:
A public-sector bank moves its branches to new software. Clerks who ran the old system for years now take far longer with each customer. They do not need new jobs; they need training.

In plain wordsTraining teaches people the skills they need to do their present job better.

Exam definitionTraining is the act of increasing the knowledge and skill of an employee for doing a particular job (Edwin Flippo). A fuller textbook version: a systematic process of enhancing employees' skills, knowledge and competencies to improve performance in their current job.

Training focuses on practical application, specific abilities and work efficiency. Done well, it raises productivity and quality and lowers operational costs. It happens in two settings.

On-the-job training happens at the workplace, during real work:

On-the-job methodKey focusAn illustration
CoachingOne-to-one instruction in job skillsA senior clerk sits beside a new clerk at the counter for a week
Job rotationExperience across departments or tasksA probationary officer spends a few months each in deposits, loans and cash
MentoringLong-term guidance by a seniorA branch manager guides a young officer through her first year
InternshipsPractical work experienceA commerce student works at the branch for eight weeks
ApprenticeshipsLong-term, skill-based trainingAt an auto-parts plant, a trainee fitter learns the trade over a long period under a qualified fitter

Off-the-job training takes place outside the normal work environment, through theory or simulation: classroom training, seminars and workshops, e-learning, simulation exercises and case studies. One classic form is vestibule training: a separate training area with the same equipment as the real job, such as a mock counter with the new software at the bank's staff college.

SettingStrengthsWeaknesses
On the jobReal conditions; the trainee produces while learning; low costMistakes reach real customers; a skilled worker may be a poor teacher
Off the jobNo pressure from customers; structured; safe to make mistakesCosts more; time away from work; harder to carry back to the job

Don't confuse coaching with mentoring. Coaching is short and specific: how to do this task well. Mentoring is long-term guidance by a senior, often about the person's career as well as the job.

Where it breaks. Training only fixes a gap in skill or knowledge. If people are slow because the computers freeze, targets are unclear, or morale is low, a course will not help. What is learnt off the job also fades unless managers let people use it at work.

For exams. Expect to sort methods into on-the-job and off-the-job. Vestibule training is off the job, even though it uses real equipment.

blocks.title: The training process
blocks.html:
A company sends all 200 of its sales staff to a two-day negotiation workshop. Sales do not move, because the real problem was late deliveries. Training that starts without asking what is wrong often teaches the wrong thing.

In plain wordsThe training process is the order in which training is planned, given and checked, starting with who needs to learn what.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: training needs analysis identifies the gap between the knowledge and skills employees have and those their jobs require. McGehee and Thayer's classic model analyses needs at three levels: the organisation, the task and the person.

StepWhat happens
1 Identify training needsFind performance gaps and skill shortages
2 Determine participantsSelect the employees who need training
3 Prepare learnersBuild readiness and interest
4 Present the operationDemonstrate the task clearly
5 Performance try-outTrainees perform under supervision
6 Follow-upEvaluate, correct errors and make sure it is applied

Steps 3 to 6 are the classic four-step job instruction training method: prepare, present, try out, follow up. It was spread widely by the United States' Training Within Industry programme during the Second World War.

An illustration: a supermarket before its Diwali sale.

  1. Needs: billing errors have risen to about 30 a week, mostly on discount coupons.
  2. Participants: the 12 cashiers who joined in the last three months.
  3. Prepare: the supervisor explains why errors cost the store and puts the cashiers at ease.
  4. Present: she bills a basket with a coupon, step by step, explaining each key.
  5. Try-out: each cashier bills 20 practice items while she watches and corrects.
  6. Follow-up: she checks each cashier's errors daily for two weeks.

Evaluating the result (follow-up). The most widely taught framework has four levels:

Don't confuse a good reaction with training that worked. Trainees can enjoy a session and learn nothing, or learn and never use it. Only levels 3 and 4 show that the job has changed.

Where it breaks. The six steps fit teaching a definite task, such as billing or operating a machine. They fit less well for judgement and leadership, which take months to show. At level 4, other changes, such as a new product or a festival season, can also move the numbers.

In practice. Decide at step 1 which measure the training should change, such as errors per week. Then follow-up has something to check.

Go deeper for practitioners

Return on training. Jack Phillips added a fifth level: return on investment (ROI), which compares the money benefit with the cost.

Training ROI (%) = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost × 100

An illustration: a programme costs ₹2 lakh. Billing errors used to cost the chain ₹40,000 a month; afterwards they cost ₹15,000. The saving is ₹25,000 a month, or ₹3 lakh a year. ROI = (3 − 2) ÷ 2 × 100 = 50% in the first year.

The weak point is the benefit figure. If a new billing machine arrived at the same time, part of the saving is not training's. Comparing trained stores with similar untrained stores over the same months gives a fairer figure.

A decision. Your head office wants all managers on a three-day leadership course. The needs analysis shows that most complaints are about two branches with high staff turnover. Do you run the course for everyone, or start with those two branches?

Needs, participants, preparation, presentation, try-out, follow-up.

blocks.title: Development, and how it differs from training
blocks.html:
A bank's best loan officer is made branch manager, and she struggles. Nobody prepared her to lead twenty people. Training made her good at her job; development would have prepared her for the next one.

In plain wordsDevelopment grows people for the jobs they will hold later, not only the one they hold now.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: development is the process of enhancing employees' knowledge, skills and abilities for future responsibilities and long-term growth.

Development focuses on future roles, career growth, leadership potential and the talent pipeline: the flow of people being readied for bigger jobs. Its methods include training programmes, job rotation, job enrichment, mentoring and coaching, skill workshops, e-learning, cross-training, simulations and role-play, certifications, and feedback and appraisal. Job enrichment adds responsibility and decision-making to a job. Cross-training teaches people a colleague's job.

A development plan for the loan officer, an illustration over two years: a year in branch operations, a regional manager as mentor, a small project leading three colleagues, a leadership course, and feedback every quarter.

BasisTrainingDevelopment
FocusSpecific job-related skillsBroader career and personal growth
Time horizonShort-termLong-term
ScopeJob-specific and narrowCareer-oriented and wide
PurposeImprove current performancePrepare for future roles
MethodsOn-the-job training, workshops, seminarsMentoring, coaching, job rotation

Don't sort by method alone. Job rotation, mentoring and coaching appear under both training and development. What decides is the purpose: a skill for the present job is training; readiness for a future role is development.

Where it breaks. Development pays off later and is hard to measure, so it is often the first budget cut in a bad year. Employers also worry that people they develop will leave. The opposite risk is also real: no one ready when a key person goes, which is the gap succession planning exists to fill.

For exams. Learn the table, and the one-line version: training is job-oriented and short-term; development is career-oriented and long-term.

Training is for current performance; development is for future growth.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says: learn thoroughly what is worth learning, and then stand by it. The training process ends the same way, with a follow-up that checks whether what was learnt is being applied.
pairings.quote: “Learn thoroughly what should be learnt, and having learnt it, live by it.” கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை கற்றபின் நிற்க அதற்குத் தக. Tirukkuṟaḷ 391

text: The deeper a well is dug in sand, the more water flows into it; the more a person learns, the more their knowledge grows. Development, unlike training, is open-ended growth of exactly this kind.
pairings.quote: “As water springs in a sand well the deeper it is dug, so knowledge springs the more one learns.” தொட்டனைத் தூறும் மணற்கேணி மாந்தர்க்குக் கற்றனைத் தூறும் அறிவு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 396

chapters.title: Job Analysis, Evaluation and Design
chapters.scope: Studying jobs, writing them down, judging their worth and shaping them: analyse, document, evaluate, design.

blocks.title: Job analysis and its methods
blocks.html:
An auto-parts plant in Pune needs twenty new machine operators. Before it can advertise, test candidates or fix their pay, someone has to know exactly what an operator does all day, and what it takes to do it well.

In plain wordsJob analysis is finding out, carefully and on purpose, what a job involves and what kind of person can do it.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: job analysis is a systematic study of a job to find the tasks, methods, equipment, skills and attitudes needed for successful performance.

Job analysis yields four kinds of information:

  • Purpose and nature: why the job exists and what it involves.
  • Organisational fit: its department, reporting line and place in the hierarchy.
  • Human profile: the skills, attributes and behaviour it needs.
  • Relationships and context: whom the jobholder deals with, what they depend on, the tools they use and the demands they face.

Back to the plant. As an illustration, an analyst watches operators for a week, interviews two supervisors, and collects accounts of the best and worst shifts. She finds that most of an operator's day goes on setting machines, and that the costliest mistakes happen at shift change. That one finding shapes the job advertisement, the selection test and the training plan.

Methods. No single method sees everything, so most analyses combine two or more.

MethodKey focusWatch out for
Direct observationWatching employees at work; best for routine or physical jobsIt misses thinking work, and people may act differently when watched
Work method analysisTime and motion study to find the most efficient sequenceIt suits repetitive manual work; staff may resent being timed
Critical incident techniqueAnalysing exceptionally effective or ineffective incidentsIt shows the extremes, not the ordinary day
Interview methodEmployees and supervisors describe the job in detailPeople may make their job sound bigger than it is

Textbooks also list questionnaires and work diaries, in which jobholders record what they do over a period.

Strategic uses. Job analysis supports work simplification (breaking complex jobs into manageable tasks), sets measurable performance standards, and supports recruitment, selection, training and appraisal.

Don't confuse job analysis with job evaluation. Analysis describes what a job is and what it needs. Evaluation judges what the job is worth compared with other jobs. Analysis comes first and feeds evaluation.

Where it breaks. Jobs change faster than documents. In fast-moving roles, a careful analysis can be out of date within a year. Each method also has a blind spot, as the table shows.

For exams. Expect to match a method to its description. The critical incident technique is linked with John Flanagan (1954); time study with F. W. Taylor; motion study with Frank and Lillian Gilbreth.

A limit of observation: people may behave differently when watched (the Hawthorne effect).

blocks.title: Job description and job specification
blocks.html:
A bank branch advertises for "a smart, hardworking officer". Two hundred people apply, and most are wrong for the job. A clear job description and job specification would have filtered them out before anyone read a CV.

In plain wordsThe job description says what the job is. The job specification says what the person doing it must have.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a job description is a written statement of what the jobholder does, how, and under what conditions; a job specification states the minimum qualifications, experience, skills and personal qualities needed to do the job.

Both are written from the findings of job analysis. One looks at the work; the other looks at the worker.

Job description: defines the jobJob specification: defines the person
Job purpose and summaryRequired qualifications
Tasks and dutiesExperience
Reporting line and locationMental and physical attributes
Working conditionsEmotional traits
Tools and responsibilitiesTechnical and interpersonal skills

An example. Here is an illustration for a counter supervisor at a public-sector bank branch.

Job descriptionJob specification
Purpose: keep the cash counters accurate and the queues movingA graduate, with three years as a cashier
Duties: supervise four cashiers, approve large withdrawals, balance cash at closeConfident with the core banking software
Reports to the branch manager; based at the branchSpeaks the local language with customers
Works on the counter floor, with peak rush on MondaysStays calm and polite under pressure from a long queue

How they are used. The description becomes the job advertisement, the induction plan and the base for appraisal goals. The specification becomes the screening checklist and the interview plan.

Don't confuse the two. A common slip is to put "three years' experience" in the description. Anything about the person goes in the specification; anything about the work goes in the description.

Where it breaks. A rigid description invites "not my job" thinking, so many firms write broader role profiles. A specification can be inflated, such as a postgraduate degree for data entry. That shrinks the pool of applicants and can shut out people who could do the job well.

In practice. Test each line of the specification against the description: which duty needs this? If no duty needs it, drop it.

The job description says what the job involves; the job specification says who can do it.

blocks.title: Job evaluation and its methods
blocks.html:
At a milk cooperative, the lab chemist earns less than the truck dispatcher and asks why. Without a method for comparing jobs, the only answer is "that is how it has always been", and that answer breeds resentment.

In plain wordsJob evaluation compares jobs, not the people in them, to decide which jobs are worth more, so that pay can be set in a fair order.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: job evaluation is a systematic, comparative process of determining the relative worth of jobs within an organisation.

Objectives. Internal equity, so that jobs of similar worth get fair pay; a standard pay structure; fairness, with less favouritism and wage inequality; and benchmarking against industry pay.

The process runs in four steps:

Job analysis → job documentation → job rating → job hierarchy

Study each job, write it up, rate it with one of the methods below, then arrange the jobs in order and group them into grades. Pay ranges are attached to the grades afterwards.

MethodKindCore idea
RankingNon-quantitativeCompare and rank jobs by overall worth
Grading or classificationNon-quantitativePlace jobs into predefined grades
Points systemQuantitativeWeight compensable factors and assign points
Factor comparisonQuantitativeCompare jobs with benchmark jobs, factor by factor

The points system, worked. A compensable factor is a feature of a job that the organisation is willing to pay for. Say the cooperative uses four, each with five levels. The maximum points show each factor's weight.

FactorMaximum pointsPoints per level (5 levels)
Skill40080
Responsibility30060
Effort20040
Working conditions10020

A panel rates each job on each factor:

  • Lab chemist: skill level 5 (400), responsibility 4 (240), effort 2 (80), conditions 3 (60). Total 780.
  • Truck dispatcher: skill 3 (240), responsibility 3 (180), effort 3 (120), conditions 2 (40). Total 580.
  • Packing-line worker: skill 1 (80), responsibility 1 (60), effort 4 (160), conditions 4 (80). Total 380.

The chemist's job ranks highest. If grades are set at 700 points and above, 500 to 699, and below 500, the three jobs fall into three different grades. The chemist's complaint was justified.

Factor comparison works differently. It starts with benchmark jobs whose pay is accepted as fair, splits that pay across the factors, and then slots other jobs in factor by factor.

Don't confuse job evaluation with performance appraisal. Evaluation rates the job; appraisal rates how well a person does it. Two operators in the same job share one job value but can get different appraisal ratings.

Where it breaks. Choosing the factors and their weights is a judgement, so bias can enter dressed up as numbers. Evaluation sets the internal order, but the job market can pull against it when a skill is scarce. And it needs redoing as jobs change.

For exams. Know which methods are quantitative, the order of the process, and the three objectives of equity, structure and benchmarking.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Your evaluation puts the dispatcher's job one grade below a stores clerk's. But dispatchers are hard to hire, and the market pays them more. Raising the job's grade would distort the structure for everyone. A common answer is to keep the grade and pay a separate market allowance, reviewed each year. Then the structure stays honest, and the extra pay can be removed if the market changes.

Widely used schemes. Textbooks describe the points system as the most widely used method. The Hay method, from the consultancy Hay Group, is a well-known points-factor scheme built on know-how, problem solving and accountability.

Links. Compensation management (this unit) builds pay ranges on the grades. The equity objective connects to Adams's equity theory in the motivation chapter: people compare what they get for their effort with what others get.

Non-quantitative methods compare whole jobs; quantitative ones score factors.

blocks.title: Job design
blocks.html:
A garment unit splits shirt-making into thirty tiny steps. Output rises at first, but so do absences: people who stitch one collar seam all day get bored and leave. How tasks are bundled into jobs matters.

In plain wordsJob design is deciding which tasks go into a job and how much say the person has over them.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: job design is structuring jobs to achieve organisational efficiency while meeting employees' motivational needs.

MethodWhat it does
Job simplificationFewer, repetitive tasks: more efficiency, but possible monotony
Job rotationMoves people across roles: less boredom, more versatility
Job enlargementHorizontal expansion: more tasks at the same level
Job enrichmentVertical expansion: more responsibility, autonomy and decision-making

An example. In a bank's loan section, a clerk only types application data into the system. That is a simplified job.

  • Rotation: the clerk spends three months each in deposits, loans and foreign exchange.
  • Enlargement: the clerk now enters the data, checks the documents and files them. There are more tasks, all at the same level.
  • Enrichment: the clerk handles small loans from start to finish and can approve them up to a set limit. The job now carries responsibility.

Don't confuse enlargement with enrichment. Enlargement is horizontal: more of the same kind of work. Enrichment is vertical: more control over the work. Frederick Herzberg warned that piling on more routine tasks ("horizontal job loading") does not motivate.

Where it breaks. Enrichment does not suit everyone; some people prefer clear, routine work. It also needs training, and people given more responsibility often expect more pay. Simplification still suits high-volume, standardised work done by new staff.

In practice. Match the method to the problem. Boredom calls for rotation or enlargement. Capable staff with little ownership call for enrichment. Frequent errors in high-volume work may call for simplification.

Go deeper for practitioners

The job characteristics model. J. Richard Hackman and Greg Oldham (1975) named five core features of a motivating job: skill variety, task identity (doing a whole piece of work), task significance, autonomy and feedback. These create three psychological states: work that feels meaningful, a sense of responsibility for outcomes, and knowledge of results.

They combined the five into a motivating potential score (MPS), each feature rated from 1 to 7:

MPS = [(skill variety + task identity + task significance) ÷ 3] × autonomy × feedback

For the typing clerk, say variety 2, identity 2, significance 5, autonomy 2 and feedback 3. MPS = (9 ÷ 3) × 2 × 3 = 18. After enrichment, say variety 5, identity 6, significance 5, autonomy 5 and feedback 5. MPS = (16 ÷ 3) × 5 × 5 ≈ 133. Autonomy and feedback multiply, so a job low on either scores low however varied it is.

Links. Enrichment grows out of Herzberg's two-factor theory in the motivation chapter: achievement, responsibility and the work itself are motivators.

Simplification: fewer tasks. Rotation: different tasks. Enlargement: more tasks. Enrichment: more authority.

text: Book 5 of the Arthaśāstra sets out a scale of annual salaries for the state's servants, from the highest officers down to labourers, graded by the importance of the post. That is a pay structure built on judging the worth of each job, which is the aim of job evaluation.

pairings.classic: making the capable the master of the work
text: The Kuṟaḷ says that once a person has been found fit for a task, they should be made its master. Job enrichment gives a capable employee more responsibility, autonomy and say over their work. The couplet is about appointing officers, so the link is offered as a reading.
pairings.quote: “Once you have found a person fit for the work, make them its master.” வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை அவனை அதற்குரிய னாகச் செயல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 518

chapters.title: Compensation Management
chapters.scope: Rewarding people for their contribution: the aims of pay, protection for injury at work, and the classic incentive plans.

blocks.title: Meaning and objectives of compensation
blocks.html:
A small software firm in Pune pays its developers ₹6 lakh a year. A rival offers ₹7.5 lakh, and three developers leave in one month. Pay decides who joins, who stays and how hard people work.

In plain wordsCompensation is everything an employer gives people in return for their work: money, and rewards that are not money.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: compensation management is the systematic process of rewarding employees for their contribution, through monetary and non-monetary rewards.

Rewards come in two kinds.

Kind of rewardWhat it includesAn illustration
Monetary rewardsWages, incentives, bonusesA monthly wage; extra pay for each order packed above target; a Diwali bonus
Non-monetary rewardsBenefits, recognition, perksMedical insurance for the family; the manager's praise at the monthly meeting; a free canteen lunch or a company bus

A pay system is designed to do six jobs at once. These are the objectives of compensation management.

ObjectiveWhat it meansIn the Pune firm
Attract talentOffer enough to bring good people inCheck what rivals offer new developers
Retain employeesGive people reasons to stayReview pay each year against the market
Motivate performanceLink part of pay to resultsA bonus for projects delivered on time
Ensure equityPay fairly, inside and outside the firmTwo developers in the same grade with the same results get similar pay
Improve productivityReward output, not only attendanceIncentive plans that pay for time saved (see the last concept)
Comply with the lawMeet every legal duty on pay and benefitsIncluding compensation for injury at work (next concept)

Equity has two sides. Internal equity means jobs inside the firm are paid fairly against each other; job evaluation ranks them for this. External equity means pay is fair against what other employers pay for similar work. The Pune firm lost its developers on external equity.

Don't confuse compensation with salary. A salary or wage is one monetary part. Compensation is the whole package, including bonuses, benefits, recognition and perks. Two job offers with the same salary can differ widely in compensation.

Where it breaks. The objectives pull against each other. Paying above the market attracts people but raises costs. Large individual bonuses motivate some people but can look unfair to colleagues. In Herzberg's two-factor theory, pay is a hygiene factor: poor pay causes dissatisfaction, but good pay alone does not create lasting motivation.

In practice. Before changing pay, find which objective is failing. If people will not join, compare pay with the market. If they join and then leave, check equity. If they stay but coast, look at how pay links to performance.

For exams. Learn the six objectives, and sort rewards as monetary or non-monetary. Equity links to job evaluation and to Adams's equity theory (the organisational justice chapter).

blocks.title: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923
blocks.html:
A press operator at an auto-parts plant in Pune loses two fingers in an accident during his shift. He cannot do his old work, and his family lives on his wage. The law decides what the employer owes him.

In plain wordsIf work injures or kills an employee, or makes them ill, the employer must pay compensation to the employee or the family.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 gives financial protection to employees who are injured during their employment or who suffer occupational diseases, by making the employer liable to pay compensation.

The Act was first called the Workmen's Compensation Act; an amendment in 2009 gave it its present name. Here compensation means a payment for injury, disease or death, not pay for work.

The key test. The employer is liable for injury "arising out of and in the course of employment". Both parts must hold. In the course of employment means the injury happened during the employment, at a time and place connected with the job. Arising out of employment means the work caused it. The press accident passes both tests. A fall at home on a Sunday passes neither.

ProvisionWhat it means
Employer liabilityCompensation for injury arising out of and in the course of employment
CoverageAccidents, occupational diseases and employment-related death
DependantsCompensation to the widow, children and other eligible dependants
Medical examinationMay be required to assess the injury or disability
Notice and claimsAccidents should be reported promptly
Non-complianceFines, and a penalty with interest for late payment of compensation

How much is paid. The amount depends on the injury, the percentage of disability, and the worker's monthly wage and age. Age enters through a statutory "relevant factor". So two workers with the same injury can receive different amounts.

The Act today. The Code on Social Security, 2020 came into force on 21 November 2025. It repeals this Act and carries its provisions into the Code, along with eight other social security laws.

Don't confuse the two meanings of compensation. In compensation management, compensation is the reward for work. Under this Act, it is a payment for harm caused by work. An exam question about compensation for an accident is about this Act.

Where it breaks. The worker or the family must show that the injury arose out of and in the course of employment, and many disputes turn on that question. Occupational diseases are harder still, because they develop slowly and the link to work is harder to prove. And compensation pays for harm after it happens; only safety at work prevents it.

In practice. Report accidents promptly, keep records, and help the claim along. Late payment brings a penalty with interest, so delay only costs the employer more.

For exams. Know the phrase "arising out of and in the course of employment", who can claim, and what the amount depends on. Know that the Code on Social Security, 2020 now replaces the Act.

blocks.title: Incentive plans
blocks.html:
An auto-parts plant in Pune pays machinists by the hour. The fast ones earn exactly what the slow ones earn, so after a while nobody hurries. Incentive plans pay extra for doing the work faster or better.

In plain wordsAn incentive plan pays people more when they produce more, or finish faster, than a set standard.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: incentive plans link reward to performance, measured as productivity, efficiency or time saved.

The idea runs both ways: higher efficiency brings higher earnings, and higher earnings encourage higher productivity. Most classic plans start from a standard time for a job, set by work study, and pay a bonus for time saved. In the formulas, T is the time taken, S the standard time and R the hourly rate.

PlanDeveloperPrinciple
Halsey premium planF. A. HalseyTime wage plus 50% of the time saved
Bedaux planCharles BedauxGuaranteed base pay plus a bonus based on Bedaux points; calculation is complex and may cause disputes
Rowan planJames RowanBonus = time wage × (time saved ÷ standard time); the bonus rises until half the standard time is saved, then falls, so earnings per hour can never reach double the time rate
Emerson's efficiency planHarrington EmersonGuaranteed daily wage plus a bonus that starts at two-thirds efficiency and rises with it
Gantt task and bonus systemH. L. GanttGuaranteed time rate, plus a fixed bonus for meeting or beating the standard
Taylor's differential piece rateF. W. TaylorTwo piece rates: higher above the standard, lower below it; a strong incentive that may cause stress
Halsey: Earnings = T × R + 50% × (S − T) × R
Rowan: Earnings = T × R + ((S − T) ÷ S) × T × R

A worked example. A machinist at the Pune plant gets a job with a standard time of 10 hours. He finishes in 6 hours, and his rate is ₹50 an hour. So S = 10, T = 6, R = 50, and the time saved, S − T, is 4 hours.

  • Time wage: T × R = 6 × 50 = ₹300.
  • Halsey: bonus = 50% × 4 × 50 = ₹100. Earnings = 300 + 100 = ₹400.
  • Rowan: bonus = (4 ÷ 10) × 6 × 50 = 0.4 × 300 = ₹120. Earnings = 300 + 120 = ₹420.

Had he taken the full 10 hours, the job would have cost ₹500, so both plans save the employer money. Both also pay the worker more per hour: ₹66.67 under Halsey (400 ÷ 6) and ₹70 under Rowan (420 ÷ 6). Under Halsey, the ₹200 value of the 4 hours saved is split equally between worker and employer.

Halsey or Rowan: which pays more? It depends on how much time is saved.

When less than half the standard time is saved, Rowan pays more. At exactly half, they pay the same: with T = 5, both give ₹375. When more than half is saved, Halsey pays more: with T = 4, Halsey gives ₹350 and Rowan ₹320. Rowan's falling bonus protects the employer if a standard time was set too loosely.

Don't confuse Halsey's bonus with Rowan's. Halsey's bonus is a fixed share, 50%, of the time saved, valued at the hourly rate. Rowan's bonus is the time wage multiplied by the fraction of standard time saved. A common slip is to multiply Rowan's fraction by the standard time instead of the time taken. Note too that every plan here guarantees a time wage except Taylor's, which pays only by piece rate.

Where it breaks. Every plan depends on a fair standard time. A loose standard overpays; a tight one angers workers, who then ignore the plan. Rewarding speed can cut quality and safety unless output is inspected. A plan workers cannot check, such as Bedaux, invites disputes. Individual plans suit measurable, repeated work, not team work or knowledge work.

For exams. Expect to match each plan to its developer, and to calculate Halsey and Rowan earnings.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why Rowan's hourly rate can never double. Divide Rowan earnings by the time taken: the rate earned per hour is R × (2 − T ÷ S). As T falls toward zero, that rate approaches 2R but never reaches it. Halsey has no such ceiling. A worker who saves more than two-thirds of the standard time earns over double the hourly rate.

Emerson's efficiency. Efficiency is standard time ÷ time taken × 100. In the version most textbooks give, the bonus begins at 66⅔% efficiency and reaches 20% of the time wage at 100%. Above 100%, it rises by a further 1% for each 1% of efficiency.

A decision. Your plant's standard times were set five years ago, before new machines arrived. Workers now save 60% of standard time, so Halsey pays them 1.75 times the hourly rate. Rowan would pay 1.6 times. Do you switch to Rowan, or re-time the jobs? Re-timing fixes the cause; switching plans only limits the cost. Either change is best agreed with the workers first, or it may start a dispute.

Links. Taylor's differential piece rate belongs to scientific management, in the classical school (the organisational behaviour chapter).

text: The Kuṟaḷ says that even when fate denies success, effort still earns the wages of one's labour. Compensation management starts from a related point: contribution is owed a reward. The couplet is about the worth of effort itself, not an employer's duty to pay, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Even when fate denies the result, effort yields the wages of one's labour.” தெய்வத்தான் ஆகா தெனினும் முயற்சிதன் மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 619

text: In the same chapter as its salary scale, the Arthaśāstra provides that when servants die in the course of their work, their sons and wives are to receive their food and wages. The Employees' Compensation Act gives a worker's dependants a comparable claim.

chapters.title: Strategic Human Resource Management
chapters.scope: Aligning HR with the organisation's strategy, so that its people become a lasting source of advantage.

blocks.title: Meaning of strategic HRM
blocks.html:
Strategic human resource management (SHRM) aligns HR activities (recruitment, training, performance management and development) with the organisation's strategy.

HR activities → strategic alignment → workforce capability → competitive advantage
  • Employees are treated as long-term strategic assets.
  • HR becomes proactive, helping shape the organisation's growth and capability.
  • The focus shifts from routine HR administration to strategic people management.

blocks.title: Key strategic dimensions
blocks.html:
DimensionWhat it involves
Employer branding and talent acquisitionCommunicate the culture to attract talent; a strong brand brings better applicants and fewer mismatches
Employee lifecycle managementOnboarding, development, engagement and retention; lower turnover and a stable workforce
Performance and learningPerformance management that focuses on growth, not fault-finding; continuous learning
Retention and engagementGrowth opportunities, recognition and fairness; analyse why people leave
Culture and change managementReinforce values and behaviour; people-focused change meets less resistance

blocks.title: Components and objectives of SHRM
blocks.html:
ComponentMeaning
Human resources as core capitalSkills and potential
HR policies and programmesMotivate and align employees
Plans and patternsStrategic planning and consistent behaviour
Unified directionHR actions aligned with the long-term vision
SHRM = people capability + HR systems + strategic direction
ObjectiveMeans
Strategic fitAlignment of HR with strategy and its execution
Resource-based strategySpecialised talent as a competitive advantage
High-performance managementMeasures and productivity
High-involvement managementSharing ideas, innovation
High-commitment managementTrust and employee dedication

Fit, resource, performance, involvement, commitment.

blocks.title: Implementing SHRM
blocks.html:
Implementation stepWhat it involves
1 Understand the business visionAlign HR with purpose and the strategic plan
2 Identify measures and dataUse people analytics; data-driven decisions reduce bias
3 Assess HR readinessReview skills, structure and technology; close the gaps
4 Forecast talent needsPredict needs for growth or automation; reskill and upskill
5 Assess HR systemsMake HR tools efficient and integrated
6 Evaluate and iterateMonitor outcomes and keep policies relevant

Strategic HR planning runs in five steps: define SMART goals, assess HR capabilities, evaluate workforce skills, analyse departmental needs, and recruit strategically for cultural fit, adaptability and future readiness.

The right people, with the right capabilities, for the right strategy, at the right time.

text: The Kuṟaḷ tells the ruler to look every day into the conduct of those who do his work: if they do not swerve, the world will not swerve. SHRM's last step, evaluating and iterating, is the same discipline of regular review.
pairings.quote: “Let the ruler look daily into the conduct of those who work for him; if they do not swerve, the world will not swerve.” நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான் கோடாமை கோடா துலகு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 520
